# Remote query cache history

Record remote queries, result caching, and multi-select paste in the same history, but don't treat them as a single implementation. All we can confirm at this point is that the first two both affect which results the dropdown component sees and where to start a review. For multi-select paste, we only have a name to investigate; that isn't enough to document callback timing or parameters.

Two ways of recording this were initially compared.

- Keep caching entirely with the query entry point. When the list doesn't change, follow the query path to find out why.
- Record normal result reuse and temporary refresh separately. The query remains one entry point, while temporarily not reusing old results is treated as a state that ends.

Tentatively use the second approach. This isn't intended to add a request protocol, just to avoid interpreting "no update this time" as caching. A new query may never have started, candidate results may not have been retained, or existing results may indeed have been reused. These possibilities can't be conflated based on the same symptom.

Record `dist/components/dropdown.js` as the place to start reviewing. This was only where the investigation could continue at the time; it doesn't mean the state is necessarily held there. If a later review finds that result reuse is decided somewhere adjacent, correct this record rather than insisting that the path identifies the implementation owner.

Leave multi-select paste out of the decision for now. The early guess was that it would probably go through the query entry point, so it could be filled in once the remote query baseline was stable. That guess was only a scheduling convenience, not a behavioral commitment. If it only changes selected values, or makes no remote request at all, it shouldn't be used to extend the caching discussion.

Decision: keep remote queries and caching on the same history line; retain multi-select paste as an adjacent issue. The next review should record separate observations for normal queries, reuse of existing results, and temporary refresh, rather than leaving only "the list didn't change."

# Remote Query Cache History

The first version documented remote queries, result caching, and multi-select paste together. The intent was to keep the investigation at the time from missing adjacent entry points. Looking back, that arrangement created an unnecessary implication: items on the same page were easily read as parts of the same behavioral chain. This revision keeps the earlier judgments, but separates the scope settled at the time from the items that remained unresolved.

## The original choice still stands

The two early options remain. One was to treat caching entirely as a query-entry issue: when the list did not update, explain it in terms of whether the query had run again. The other was to treat result reuse as the norm, and temporary refresh as a state meant to apply to just one query opportunity. We are continuing with the latter.

The reason is not that we already know every code path, but that these are two different intents. Normal reuse concerns whether existing remote results can be retained; temporary refresh concerns a particular operation that should not reuse old results. Combining them into "cache on or off" strips the investigation record of its temporal boundaries. If someone writes only "already cleared" without specifying whether this is meant to affect just the current operation or all subsequent operations, contradictory interpretations follow.

This decision only specifies how to document the behavior. It does not require callers to split it into multiple actions. There is still one query entry point; whether results are retained and whether a temporary refresh is needed are different questions about that same entry point. Separating them allows a review to identify which behavior actually occurred.

## Three issues exposed during review

One review broke the vague label "caching anomaly" into three questions: did the search start, under what conditions were candidates retained after it started, and could existing results be reused this time? This is not a new interface proposal. It is a way to stop inferring every cause from the final list.

An unchanged list can mean at least three things. If the search did not start automatically, the page has no new results to compare; if candidates did not meet the matching conditions, the display may also remain blank or show old content; if existing remote results were reused, the UI presents yet another similar case of "no change." The previous version did not distinguish these cases. As a result, some people took a search not starting to mean the cache had not been cleared, while others took results not being retained to mean old results were still there.

The clearest disagreement concerned multi-word searches. One view was that results could be retained as long as some related content could be found in the configured fields for every word. The other view was stricter: observing different words in different candidates must not be recorded as though a single result had satisfied the entire query. This disagreement was about matching, not remote result reuse. At the time, however, it got mixed into the caching discussion because both were described as "can't find it."

Auto-start was also misunderstood. Someone disabled auto-start but still saw the previous list, and concluded that the caching logic was not respecting the setting. That observation does not directly support the conclusion: auto-start describes when a search is initiated, while whether existing content remains on screen is a different matter. Conversely, a change after a manual trigger does not automatically prove that the cache had been bypassed earlier.

## Multi-select paste is not a caching branch

During review, someone suggested including multi-select paste in the second paragraph on result reuse because it changes the dropdown's current value. That suggestion was not adopted. A change to the current value is not the same as whether remote candidate results are read, and neither "multi-select" nor "paste" alone establishes that a temporary refresh has occurred.

The first version's statement that "paste probably goes through the same query entry point" remains where it was, but is no longer used as a basis for judgment. There were no corresponding observations of calls at the time; it merely placed items to investigate side by side in a narrowly scoped record. The more appropriate boundary is this: multi-select paste remains an adjacent issue and enters this decision's scope only when it is confirmed to actually affect remote queries.

This also explains why the current value cannot serve as evidence for a caching conclusion. The value may come from paste, while the candidate list may come from earlier results. Appearing on the same screen does not establish that they share state. The early record put them on one page for ease of lookup. That historical reason should be retained, rather than retroactively adding a relationship that does not exist.

## Retired observation sequence

Early reviews used a convenient shortcut: operate the component, then inspect the final list; if the list had not changed, suspect caching first. This remains here as an old procedure, but is no longer suitable as a basis for conclusions.

The problem is not that observing the list is useless, but that the list collapses startup, matching, and reuse into one result. Without auto-start, no new search can be observed; different matching conditions produce different candidates; and reusing existing results may also happen to leave the page looking unchanged. A single final display cannot rank these three possibilities.

The replacement record need not be long. During review, first state the observation concretely, for example, "No search started this time" or "Existing remote results were still displayed this time." These statements are not interchangeable. The former does not establish result reuse, and the latter does not establish whether auto-start was enabled.

## Provisional decision

Remote queries and caching will continue to share one history, but "caching issue" must no longer be used to cover every search anomaly. Records should first identify whether the observation concerns triggering, matching, or reuse, then discuss whether there was an intent to temporarily refresh. This retains the original entry point while separating the three judgments most easily confused.

The old interpretation also included an overextension: some believed that after one refresh, all subsequent remote queries should keep avoiding old results until reinitialization. This is inconsistent with the first version's choice to treat refresh as a bounded state, so it is not being adopted at this point. It remains on the page because earlier investigation notes used this kind of language, and readers need to know why the later misreading that "refresh stays in effect forever" arose.

Two questions remain unanswered: what identifiable result Multi-Select Paste Callback produces in current regression testing; and whether temporary refresh has already been consumed on paths where no actual remote query occurs. Cache semantics cannot fill in the former, and the latter cannot be settled solely from what the UI displays.

# Remote Query Cache History Log

This record originally only left the dropdown component a place where investigation could continue. Remote querying, result caching, and multi-select paste were mentioned in the same round of wrap-up, so they were first written on one page. On rereading it later, what is truly worth preserving is not several parallel terms, but how the old record described search initiation, result matching, reuse of existing results, and current-value changes as one thing.

The current location that can still be looked up is `dist/components/dropdown.js`. It served as an entry point during the early investigation, but should not therefore carry attribution decisions for all adjacent behaviors. Some of the old sections below no longer apply; they are retained not to repackage the old wording as current documentation, but so that people who later see the same wording know where the misinterpretation began.

---

## The Initial Narrow Record

Very few observations were left at first: candidate results after a remote query seemed to appear again during the next operation; multi-select paste was mentioned, but there was no material showing whether it initiated a query. At that time, there was no way to draw the complete call relationship, and no reason to treat the two as the same mechanism.

So the first version made only one scope decision. Remote querying and result caching could continue to be recorded along the same historical thread because both concerned the source of candidate results; multi-select paste was kept to the side because it was then only a callback name awaiting investigation. This decision did not claim that paste would not touch querying, nor did it claim that a value change would necessarily produce a remote request.

Two ways of writing it were compared at the time. The first completely merged caching into the query entry point: when the list did not update, first ask whether the query had happened again. It was concise and suitable for ad hoc investigation, but it would blend together the several causes of "no new list."

The second recorded ordinary result reuse and temporary refresh separately. The query still originated from the existing entry point; ordinary reuse described whether existing results could continue to be used; temporary refresh described when old results should not be reused for a particular opportunity. The second option was chosen because it could at least ask one concrete question: why should the previous result not be reused this time, and why did things return to normal afterward?

The first version did not treat this choice as a new protocol. "Separately" meant asking separately in the record and review; it did not require callers to artificially split the operation into two requests, nor did it mean that the component necessarily had an independent long-lived switch. The only thing that could be confirmed at the time was that whether the final list changed was insufficient to explain caching on its own.

That draft also left a sentence that later caused ambiguity: "Multi-select paste probably goes through the same query entry point; fill it in together after the query baseline is stable." The value of the original sentence is that it exposed the scheduling mindset at the time: it put two unknowns together, without being based on clear behavioral observation. Later content should not rewrite this convenient grouping as an implementation fact.

## The Early Gaps Were Not Filled

The first round of records did not answer three questions: whether search started, how candidate results were judged to match, and when the intent to temporarily not reuse old results ended. These questions were later called "cache problems" in turn, causing the same UI phenomenon to bear too many explanations.

For example, an unchanged list could mean that search did not start automatically; it could also mean that no candidate satisfied the matching conditions; or it could mean that existing results continued to be used. All three situations could appear as "nothing new" on the page, but they cannot be closed out by the same conclusion. The first version only had time to leave the entry point and did not manage to separate these three layers of language.

The early record also put the dropdown's current value into a side note. The reason was simple: multi-select paste and remote querying appeared in the same round of discussion, and a value change looked very close to a result change. It was later shown that this parallelism misleads readers: the current value is one object, and the candidate result is another. Their both appearing in the dropdown component does not justify inferring shared cache state.

This section was not rewritten as a complete design because there was not enough material at the time to support that level of completeness. Preserving the gap was more consistent with the purpose of the original record than fabricating a seemingly smooth behavior chain.

---

## The Later Review Supplement

The follow-up review did not immediately narrow the issue; instead, it exposed two opposing working assumptions. One assumption focused on whether a word could be found in a field; the other held that multiple query terms should not broaden results based only on scattered relevant content. Both sides initially described the issue as "search is wrong," so the debate was incorrectly placed under remote caching.

The supplement first split one operation into three observations: whether search started; why a candidate remained after it started; and whether existing results could be reused this time. This did not require callers to operate in three steps, nor was it a new external interface. It only kept the investigation from inferring every cause from the final list.

This split changed how things were recorded at the time. When there were no new results, the note first had to say whether "search did not start automatically" or "no candidate matched after it started," and then check whether existing results were present. The earlier notes that only said "did not refresh" could no longer show whether they were discussing triggering, matching, or reuse.

Multi-word search was the first place where the problem surfaced. Some people examined the words one at a time: as long as each word could find content in some configuration field, they concluded that results should appear. This view overlooked a boundary: different words hitting different candidate items does not mean that any one candidate item satisfies the entire query.

Another explanation was also misread. It required every word to participate in determining the result, but the early wording did not make the relationships among configuration fields clear, so some people understood it as requiring every word to land in the same field. That interpretation was equally too narrow. Both misreadings show that "finding one word" is not a sufficient description of matching.

The discussion of automatic start also took a wrong turn. Some people still saw the old list after disabling automatic start, and concluded that the setting had not taken effect or that the cache had not changed; others saw the list change after one manual operation, and concluded that the previous results must have been bypassed. Both inferences cross-used start timing and result source, and neither can prove the other.

This supplement did not delete the old observations. It only added a narrower correction beside them: the page still having a list cannot by itself show that search executed automatically this time; the page having no new list cannot by itself show that the cache is still active. This correction says less than the original "cache anomaly," but is enough to prevent the two judgments from continuing to be mixed.

## The Decision to Separate Multi-Select Paste

During the review, someone suggested putting multi-select paste into the result-reuse branch, on the grounds that pasting changes the dropdown's current value. The proposal was not accepted. Changing the current value at most shows that selection-related state may have changed; it is not enough to show that remote candidate results were read, much less that a temporary refresh was set or consumed.

The reason for rejecting it was not a denial of the importance of multi-select paste, but insufficient material. From the name "Multi-Select Paste Callback" alone, there is no way to determine whether it triggers a remote query, modifies candidate results, or only acts on selected values. Forcing it into the cache decision would make an unconfirmed object borrow another object's explanation.

Therefore, this decision keeps the original scope: multi-select paste remains an adjacent issue, awaiting an independently identifiable result; remote querying and caching handle only the relationship between candidate-result reuse and temporary refresh. This boundary is not a final ownership map, but a local decision to avoid over-inference.

An old note has a marginal comment saying "Mixed up." It was not deleted. That brief correction highlights a specific risk: parallel appearance on the page is not a causal relationship, and a change in the multi-select current value cannot be used to draw a conclusion about remote results.

---

## The Deprecated Review Action

The early investigation used a convenient sequence: operate the component first and observe whether the final list changed; if the list did not change, suspect the cache first. Its original intent is retained below, but it is no longer used as a basis for judgment.

> Old operation: When the list does not update, first attribute the problem to the cache, then go back to check search.

The problem is not that observing the list has no value, but that the list compresses the outcomes of initiation, matching, and reuse into one display. When automatic search does not occur, there is no new query to compare; when matching rules filter candidate items, the result may likewise remain unchanged; when existing remote results are reused, the UI also appears stable. A single final display cannot order these three explanations.

What replaced it later was not a lengthy procedure, but writing the observation as a concrete sentence first. "Search did not start this time" and "Existing remote results are still displayed this time" must be written down separately. The former cannot establish result reuse, and the latter cannot in turn prove whether automatic start is enabled.

This replacement also corrected a common sequence illusion. Someone would first see old content on the screen and infer that a request must not have happened; then, from not seeing new content, infer that the cache must not have been cleared. Both inferences skipped the matching conditions. If the relationship between query terms and candidate items is not written in the record, it is impossible to know whether what is missing is a new request or a valid result.

The old operation remains here because the same wording appears in old investigation materials. Deleting it would make later readers think that "an unchanged list is enough to suspect the cache" had never been formally used, which would instead make it harder to explain why some old conclusions conflict with one another.

## A Side Note Later Reversed

At one point, a stronger claim appeared: once a refresh had been performed, all subsequent remote queries should avoid previous results until the component was reinitialized. The side note was written very confidently, but was later overturned.

The problem was that "all subsequent" had no boundary. If a temporary action is extended into a permanent change, the original intent of obtaining one new result becomes a continuing alteration of the normal state. That neither explains when things recover nor aligns with the reason the first version chose a "consumable state."

The old wording is retained below:

> Deprecated: After refreshing once, subsequent queries should no longer use existing remote results until initialization occurs again.

It can explain only why someone at the time described a one-time operation as a long-lived switch; it cannot continue to be used to judge component behavior. The narrower direction retained during later maintenance is this: ordinary remote-result reuse remains part of the normal state, while temporary refresh serves only one opportunity that requires obtaining the result again.

No further request details are filled in here. The early material was not sufficient to explain how every path with no remote request handles this intent, and multi-select paste should not be pulled in just to give the old side note a boundary.

---

## The Correction Prompted by Counterexamples

One review initially recorded "no new results" as cache residue. When the materials from the same round were organized, the wording was corrected to: when automatic start is missing, no new results cannot establish that the cache is still working. This did not completely reverse the original judgment; it narrowed its applicable scope.

Another counterexample came from multi-word search. The initial observation checked each word separately and considered it sufficient that each could find related content. It was later discovered that this incorrectly recorded the case where "the words hit different results separately" as one result already satisfying the query. This aggregation is no longer accepted after the revision.

The two corrections have the same structure. Neither introduced a new module concept; they stopped using ambiguous words. When saying "not found," distinguish between not started and not matched; when saying "did not refresh," distinguish between no new result and continued reuse of an existing result. The problem in the old record was not a lack of terminology, but that one word carried too much causality.

Some early notes attempted to explain the counterexamples above through changes in the current value. This was also withdrawn. Multi-select paste and remote querying appeared during the same period, which cannot be a reason to assume that they share state. A later marginal note explicitly marked that association as mixed up, and it is no longer brought into cache judgments.

## Short Sentences from the Review Table

One internal review left no complete discussion, only three compressed requirements: a cache issue must be able to say "which occurrence"; multi-word search must be able to say "which words"; and automatic start must be able to say "whether it started." These sentences introduced no new setting and did not replace the current decision below; they merely refused to keep using one generalized "query anomaly" to cover different judgments.

The review also included a rejected proposal: write a separate review explanation for multi-select paste that ran completely in parallel with caching. It was not adopted because the available material established only its adjacency to the dropdown's current value, not a definite relationship to remote querying. Filling in a section just to make the layout orderly would only recreate the misreading already exposed by the first version.

Another reservation was that an early entry-point location is not the same as implementation ownership. `dist/components/dropdown.js` is still suitable as a starting point when looking something up, but do not infer from this path that all cache state or paste callbacks are handled in the same place. This reservation did not change the decision itself; it only limits what the old path can establish when read.

---

## Current Closure

After the old choices, review disagreements, deprecated action, and two corrections, the remote-query section retains only one clear compatibility determination: the static contract of the query entry point is: search's fullTextSearch value `all` requires every query term to hit across configuration fields; dropdown's remote `cache` can be set by `clear cache` to bypass it once; search's `automatic` switch does not change the result protocol.

This sentence puts the objects that were previously confused back in their respective places. `all` handles the requirement that multi-word queries impose on results and does not allow observations of different words landing in different results to be combined into success; `automatic` handles whether search executes automatically and does not change the conditions a result must satisfy; `cache` handles the configuration for remote-result reuse; `clear cache` is a bypass action for one opportunity.

Their appearance in the same history section does not mean that changing one changes the other three. Disabling automatic execution cannot lower the multi-word matching requirement; bypassing existing results once cannot modify the result protocol; a change in the dropdown's current value cannot by itself prove that the remote cache was used or cleared. These restrictions are precisely intended to prevent a return to the inference in the old record that "the list is still there, so the cache is the problem."

The current decision does not write multi-select paste into the static contract. It remains an adjacent object related to the dropdown's current value, but its name does not establish a definite relationship to remote querying or cache state. If an identifiable callback result becomes available later, first confirm whether it affects selection, search initiation, or the remote result; until then, do not borrow the explanation of `clear cache` to describe paste behavior.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Waiting for query
    Waiting for query --> Automatic execution: automatic
    Automatic execution --> Multi-word matching: all
    Multi-word matching --> Ordinary result reuse: cache
    Multi-word matching --> One-time bypass: clear cache
    Ordinary result reuse --> Waiting for query
    One-time bypass --> Waiting for query
```

The diagram retains only the objects already separated in this record: automatic execution, multi-word matching, ordinary reuse, and one-time bypass. It is not a flowchart for multi-select paste, and it does not add a call order that the old material never established. Its purpose is to prevent readers from again treating the four names as one master switch.

## The Two Old Examples Retained

**Old example one:** Enter two words, and consider the search successful as long as each word has appeared somewhere on the page. This example ignores the relationship between the words and the same result, and does not specify the configuration fields. It can explain why an "apparently relevant" judgment appeared early on, but it cannot serve as the current matching standard.

**Old example two:** After clearing a result once, treat every subsequent remote query as a new request. This example extends a one-time intent into a long-term state, conflicting with the cache judgment retained now. It remains in the appendix because some old investigation notes still use this language.

Neither old example needs to be corrected into a proper demonstration. The first reminds readers not to combine scattered hits into a single result; the second reminds readers not to write one refresh as a permanent state. They remain here because this page both carries the current decision and preserves the historical context that led to the old conclusions.

## Objects Not Yet Split Out

Multi-Select Paste Callback still lacks enough local material to show where it intersects with remote querying. At this stage, it is not handled as a cache branch. If further lookup is needed along this page, start from the dropdown's current value and the results left by the callback, rather than assuming in advance that it will go through the search entry point.

Another unresolved point is whether the old review wording will still write "not automatically executed" as "not matched." This is not a new feature decision, but it directly affects whether a cache judgment is triggered incorrectly. As long as these two terms continue to be mixed, the old list observation may still be written back as a cache conclusion.

# Form Error Dropdown Interface Proposal

This time, we'll first try separating form-error presentation from the upper-bound check for an "unlimited" dropdown. Both sit near compatibility regression work, but the former concerns where the error text remains on the page, while the latter concerns which layer actually continues accepting results when there is no limit. Combining them into one change would tie together two judgments that have not yet been confirmed.

On the form side, list two candidate paths for now: errors returned by the server for each field go into a centralized area on the page, while field rules retain their own nearby messages; or all errors are attached directly beside their fields. The second looks simpler, but when multiple responses are returned for the same field, it is still unclear who owns the ordering and display name, so it is not the preferred option.

During the trial, look at only three things: whether the field display name is still present in the output, whether multiple responses for the same field can still be read separately, and whether a disabled field will be mistaken for a failed field because an error is displayed. The first two determine whether the centralized area is usable; the last determines whether the display logic has touched field state.

dropdown does not set a numeric upper limit in advance. First ask the maintainer to confirm whether the check occurs during result generation, menu rendering, or caller parameter passing; until that entry point is clear, "unlimited" can be equated with neither "never truncate" nor "allow arbitrary additions."

If centralized presentation can only swallow field-level information, roll back the form portion to organizing only the server responses; if existing dependents treat unlimited behavior as an observable convention, do not add a limit to the dropdown portion in this round.

# Form Error and Dropdown API Proposal

The initial draft framed form issues as a choice between a "unified entry point or field-level messages," but that split is too coarse on review. Server errors are returned by field, and local validation also works around field configuration, but that does not mean the two must pass through the same rendering logic. Whether the page needs an overview, whether a field needs an inline message, and whether multiple responses for the same field should retain their order are three separate questions.

The review starts around `dist/components/form.js`. This is where the relationship between form commands, field configuration, and error rendering is checked; the path itself is not treated as a behavioral conclusion. The earlier assumption was that all errors would follow the same branch. The review so far does not support that, so withdraw the assumption.

The trial will retain two kinds of output. The page-level view handles server errors returned by field, while inline validation continues to provide local feedback next to the field container. This does not require the text in the two places to match; it avoids interpreting "the page has an overview" as "every field must use the same message position." `prompt` in the field rules remains a source of messages when a rule fails; the raw text returned by the server should not use it to masquerade as a local rule.

Whether inline mode is used is determined by the `inline` configuration, rather than inferred from whether the error came from the server or the browser. It will be more stable for the caller to choose the page mode first and then handle errors from each source than to change the form structure on the fly after receiving an error. In particular, when multiple messages are returned for the same field, the consolidated area should preserve their respective positions instead of concatenating them into an indistinguishable block of text beside the field.

This round's form observation points remain display labels, multiple errors, and disabled-field state. The first two determine whether consolidated output is acceptable; the last prevents the field's own validation state from being changed just to display an error. This does not require local rules and server responses to share the same message, nor does it treat visual consistency on the page as a compatibility goal.

Keep the dropdown portion separate. The initial draft extrapolated "no explicit upper bound" into "results are never limited"; that inference does not hold. What remains to be confirmed is not a default number, but whether the limit is held by the configuration, the remote results, or the menu itself. This round, try only the form presentation: first confirm that non-inline output can retain each server field error individually, then confirm that local messages near the fields are not displaced by the overview logic. # Form Error Dropdown API Proposal

This round narrows form rendering to a scoped, implementable proposal; dropdown limits remain under investigation. The two items were once on the same review checklist only because both appeared near compatibility regression work; the questions they actually need to answer are different. The form needs to preserve field-error readability and field-state boundaries, while the dropdown needs to establish which layer "unlimited" actually refers to for existing consumers. Hard-wiring the latter into the form proposal would only create an unsupported release condition.

The early draft assumed that as long as a server error carried a field key, it could directly reuse the local validation feedback path. That assumption is now obsolete. A field key resolves ownership; it does not determine whether the page needs an error summary, nor whether multiple responses for the same field should be collapsed or kept individually. Later, when the area around `dist/components/form.js` was reviewed, the earlier claim that "all errors use the same branch" likewise was not supported, so a unified branch is no longer a target.

What remains is not two competing implementations but two page responsibilities. Pages that need a centralized view of server responses should be able to read the displayed field and each individual error; where a field already has a local validation feedback location beside it, that location should continue to provide in-place feedback. The two can share field configuration, but shared configuration should not force them to share an output location.

The scopes compared during review were:

| Candidate | Retained | Given up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Put everything next to the field | Users do not need to look elsewhere on the page for a summary | Multiple server responses for the same field can easily lose their separation and display-name context |
| Put everything in a centralized area | Server responses can be read in one place | Feedback for local rules near the field is forced to change location |
| Keep both presentation modes | The page summary and field feedback are each retained | Callers must explicitly choose the presentation mode |

The third option is selected. Its cost is not writing another set of rules, but that error source, field ownership, and output location can no longer be combined into one switch. Field ownership is enough for the summary to find the display name; the page determines the output location. Server responses remain server responses, local rules remain local rules, and neither source rewrites the other.

These constraints are recorded here to fix the scope of observation for the form trial, not to require every page to enable the same display. The static contract for form errors is: `validate form` executes validation; `add errors` accepts field-keyed errors, the non-inline summary puts `Full Name: is already registered` and `Full Name: must be unique` into `li` separately, inline feedback lands in `.prompt`, and disabled fields do not receive the `error` state.

This constraint clarifies three ambiguities in the initial draft. First, the summary retains display labels rather than only field keys; the two server-returned messages therefore still have separate positions. Second, item-by-item output cannot compress multiple responses for the same field into an indistinguishable block. Third, a disabled field is not left unshown merely to keep the page looking clean; it must not be marked as failed in the validation state. If the page needs to display server errors, it should use the error-presentation path rather than marking a disabled field as failed to achieve a visual effect.

Field-rule message text remains solely for feedback when the rule fails. It may be fixed text or provided by a function; server-side responses should not be fed back into that rule entry. Inline configuration only determines which kind of in-place presentation field errors use; it does not determine whether server errors need a page summary. This distinction lets callers determine the page shape first and then process the two types of input separately, rather than changing the form structure ad hoc after receiving an error.

The trial order is adjusted accordingly. First run local field validation and confirm that the field rules' own feedback is unchanged; then add server responses grouped by field and check whether the summary still retains display names and individual messages; finally inspect disabled fields. The last step checks not whether the field is hidden, but whether it has been recorded as a failed state. Separating local validation from the additional server-error action is the only way to distinguish whether a difference comes from the rule, the error input, or the display mode.

FUI-202 remains the regression entry point for the form-error presentation baseline. The card's recent review record lists search terms such as field-adjacent feedback, two Full Name texts, the add-error action, field state, and the validation command, making it suitable for checking after implementation changes whether the choices here still match the behavior currently in effect. The card remains responsible for running the usual entry points and preserving terminal output and workspace side effects; this page records why those outputs are not compressed into one path.

Unlimited dropdown Limit Check was not closed out with the form conclusion. The available material only supports requiring an inventory of existing dependents and asking the module maintainer to identify entry points that can be checked further; it cannot establish the limit value, when to check, or the compatibility strategy. FUI-219 is the navigation point for this inventory. Previously treating "unlimited" as a definite statement that there was no upper limit was an inaccurate working assumption; it has now been corrected. Until the module side specifies concrete behavior, do not use this proposal to add, remove, or adjust dropdown limits.

At release, include only the form portion, and allow only an implementation in which the two presentation modes can coexist. If non-inline output cannot retain server field errors individually, fall back to leaving summary behavior unchanged; if field-adjacent feedback must depend on marking disabled fields as failed, roll back that change and recheck field-state handling. The incomplete dropdown investigation does not block form fixes within this scope, but it must not be framed as a compatibility decision that has already been made.

What remains to be confirmed is which layer owns the dropdown-limit determination and whether existing dependents treat a limit that has not been configured as observable behavior. Before these two results are available, the form regression includes no dropdown assertions.

# Popup Fallback and Calendar Troubleshooting Tree

Start by recording visible symptoms separately. Don't treat Popup mounting location and Calendar size differences as the same kind of issue.

The earliest report on the Popup side was that the caller supplied content, but no popup was visible near the expected container on the page. The working hypothesis at the time was that context might affect only positioning, not where the popup is created. There weren't enough counterexamples to support that hypothesis yet; keep it as a starting point for investigation.

```
Content does not appear
|
+-- First check whether a popup already exists on the page
|   |
|   +-- Yes: record its position relative to the trigger element and context
|   |
|   `-- No: preserve the supplied content and context value; don't change the configuration first
|
`-- Calendar size differences also appear
    |
    +-- Record only the size name and visible table width
    `-- Don't use the Popup result as evidence for Calendar
```

An old record includes a rough workaround: if the expected container can't be found, add a node with the same name and try again. This can only help distinguish "the page is missing a container" from "the component did not create one." It does not establish that the component will mount the popup under the new node. If adding a temporary node changes the symptom, retain the page structure before and after the addition. If the symptom is unchanged, stop at the call parameters; don't turn speculation into a compatibility rule.

For the Calendar issue, first retain two sets of results: the size selectors seen in one successful call and one failed call. At a minimum, record the size class, whether the date table exists, and where the width comes from. Expanding the theme variables is not required here; at the time, there was no material showing whether the difference came from selectors, variables, or call order.

Side note: empty Popup content, invisible content, and content appearing elsewhere are three different symptoms. If a later review concludes only that "it wasn't visible," that won't tell us whether to inspect mounting, content, or styles.

# Popup Fallback and Calendar Troubleshooting Tree

This review did not reuse the old approach of "adding a node with the same name will fix it." That approach can change the page conditions, but it cannot explain where the component ends up when the original context is missing. It is no longer a valid stopping criterion. The entry point is still at `dist/components/popup.min.js`. This entry point is suitable for comparing the current static output with the nodes actually left on the page, but it is not a substitute for the actual call context. Page behavior results from the interplay of call parameters, existing page nodes, and style output; opening only this one file cannot provide a complete assessment of any of them.

## The first guideline recorded in the year 2023

The initial statement was: when context cannot be found, Popup will probably still appear near the closest trigger element, so look beside the trigger element first. This was a guess that made visual inspection easier, not a confirmed rule. Its only purpose at the time was to help investigators first distinguish between "not created" and "created elsewhere".

The simplified diagram from that time is shown below, preserved as it was:

```
No content near the trigger element
|
+-- First check whether there is a Popup node
|   |
|   +-- Yes: the guess is that it may still be adjacent to the trigger element
|   `-- No: return to the call parameters
|
`-- Calendar also has size differences
    `-- First check the size classes on the page
```

This diagram did not clarify whether "adjacent" meant sharing the same parent node, being in the same context, or being somewhere else at the page root. It also did not require recording the parent node, so it can no longer be used on its own. It is retained because many records for older pages only say "not seen beside the trigger element", and interpreting those records still requires knowing how narrow the scope of observation was at the time.

Another early assumption was: missing content usually means the content value is empty. This assumption later proved invalid as well. The content value, the content area, and the result of creating the Popup itself are three different things; looking only at blank space on the screen cannot distinguish them. If an old record only says "empty content", check back to see whether the call values and node structure were also recorded.

## Operational side note in the margin

A short note was later added beside the early records: do not start by adding a context node with the same name. The reason is not that adding such a node is necessarily ineffective, but that it changes the conditions to be observed. If Popup appears after the node is added, that shows that an object that can be matched has been added to the page, but it does not reveal the original page's fallback path.

This side note led to a more practical sequence:

1. First save the result of checking whether context exists on the original page.
2. Then check whether a Popup node appears, and what its direct parent node is.
3. Only add a node when reproduction is needed; after adding it, label the result as one obtained after manually changing the page conditions.
4. Do not reduce the difference between before and after adding the node to "fixed".

During the same period, there was also an easily misunderstood side note about Calendar: a visible size name does not mean the date table is actually rendered at that size. When the page only shows the outer class, you still need to confirm whether the date table exists. If the table does not exist, there is no point in continuing to discuss width; only if the table exists but the class name does not match expectations should you enter the size selector branch.

## An inconclusive attempt

At one point, there was an attempt to troubleshoot Popup and Calendar together. The approach was to first change the page structure to make context visible, then see whether Calendar returned to the expected width. This sequence yielded no usable conclusions: changes to the page structure can affect the conditions under which Popup finds a match, but cannot explain where Calendar's size output comes from. Whether or not Calendar recovers cannot be used to verify Popup's fallback location.

The principle that emerged from this attempt was simple: both symptoms on the same page can be recorded at the same time, but each set of observations must address only one issue. Popup observations must include at least the context state for the call, the final Popup parent node, and the content area. Calendar observations must include at least the size class, the date table, and the width behavior. Do not use "both recovered" as a shared conclusion.

At the time, differences in Popup's position were also attributed to a CSS stacking issue. That attribution was not retained. Stacking affects visibility, but does not answer which parent node a node is created under; a node being obscured and a node not being in the expected container at all must be handled in separate branches. Any old notes that directly label "not visible" as a "z-index issue" should be treated as incomplete initial triage.

## Deprecated old tree

The following section comes from an old troubleshooting draft and has deliberately not been removed:

```
Expected Popup not found
|
+-- Add a node with the same name to the page
|   |
|   +-- Appears: consider the context binding issue resolved
|   `-- Does not appear: assume there is a content issue
|
`-- Calendar becomes narrower
    `-- Increase the width directly
```

**This section is deprecated.** The first branch treats the result after manually adding a node as the original behavior; the second reduces "did not appear" to a content issue; the third adjusts the width directly without first confirming the size class and date table. The old tree still has one point worth retaining: it reminds troubleshooters that Popup and Calendar symptoms often occur together. The current approach is not to ignore either one, but to split them into two separate records so that a temporary change does not contaminate both assessments at once.

## A counterexample added during review

The counterexample raised during review was this: the page already has a node with a matching name, but the context supplied in the call does not refer to it. If you search only by name and also "see Popup nearby", it is very easy to mistake an existing node or another overlay for the result of this call. Therefore, the record cannot just say "found it"; it must clearly state whether that node is the context in the call, and what Popup's immediate parent node is.

Another counterexample comes from the content area: the page may have a Popup shell without any configuration content visible. At this point, we cannot directly conclude that "the component was not created," nor can we equate a blank area with an empty content value. We should record these separately: whether the shell exists, whether the content area exists, and whether the configuration content is empty. If any one of these is missing, we can only stop at describing the observed phenomenon.

The Calendar review counterexample is more direct. A sizing class on the page does not mean that the calendar date table also received the corresponding selector; conversely, the presence of the table does not show that the theme width variable has taken effect. The sizing class, selector matching, and final width are three layers of observation. Writing them on one line will leave later reviewers unsure whether to start with the call, the style output, or the override rule.

## Branches in the current investigation

When encountering "Popup content did not appear in the expected context," start from the original page and do not fix the page first:

```
Popup symptom
|
+-- Does the node corresponding to context exist?
|   |
|   +-- No
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Popup appears on the page: record its immediate parent node and content area
|   |   `-- No Popup on the page: record the call value; stop at the creation/display conditions
|   |
|   `-- Yes
|       |
|       +-- Popup is a descendant of that node: continue checking the content area and content value
|       |
|       `-- Popup is not under that node: record the actual parent node; do not rewrite context

```
Calendar Size Selector issue
|
+-- No recognizable size class on the page
|   `-- Save the initialization inputs and page classes; stop on the caller side
|
+-- Size class present, but no date table
|   `-- Record as incomplete rendering; do not compare widths
|

|   |

|   |
|   +-- mini: check whether .ui.mini.calendar is in the style output
|   |
|   `-- Then check where the date table's min-width comes from
|

If only the outer Calendar class is present without a day table, just record that fact. If `min-width` has already been overridden elsewhere, also record "matched" and "final display differs" separately, and do not misreport the override as a missing size class.

There is currently no archived set of successful and failed calls available to replace this branch. New records should at least capture the visible results from one successful call and one failed call: the actual size class, whether the date table exists, whether the relevant selectors match, and the width behavior. There is no requirement here to extract all unrelated theme rules; the records only need to let the next person continue from the same branch point.

Previous historical records described "context not found" as "the popup probably remains near the trigger element." This wording has been explicitly withdrawn. - whether this Popup appeared on the page;
- the Popup's direct parent node;
- whether the Popup has a content area and whether that area contains the configured content;

It affects the credibility of the observation "Popup found", but it is not the Calendar Size Selector issue. It is being kept on this page for now to remind the inspector to distinguish the old node from the node created by this call first; if a stable reuse determination is established later, record it separately instead of putting it back into the context fallback branch.

Without a pairing record for the call parameters and corresponding node, stop here.

The steps below are retained only for people reading old troubleshooting records and must not be used as the current verification path:

1. Create a temporary node on the page with the same name as the expected context.
2. Trigger Popup again.
3. If the content is visible, label it as "possibly caused by missing context."
4. If Calendar also became wider, it was recorded as "styles restored."

```text
Observed symptoms
├─ Popup not in the expected area
│  ├─ Node found: record the direct parent node and content area
│  └─ Node not found: retain the context state and stop guessing the mount location
└─ Calendar dimensions differ
   ├─ Date table does not exist: stop at the rendering branch
   └─ Date table exists: separately verify the size classes and the source of min-width
```

When using this tree now, Popup and Calendar still require two separate observation records. Temporarily adding a context node changes the conditions and can only be recorded separately as a reproduction experiment; it cannot override the original page result that "the node does not exist."

If only the outer Calendar class is present and there is no day table, just record that fact. If `min-width` has already been overridden elsewhere, also record "matched" and "the final display differs" separately, and do not misrepresent an override as the absence of a size class.

There is currently no archived set of successful and failed calls available to replace this branch. New records should at least capture the visible results from one successful call and one failed call: the actual size classes, whether the date table exists, whether the relevant selectors match, and how the width behaves. There is no need to extract all unrelated theme rules here; it is enough to let the next person continue from the same fork.

## Corrections for 2025

The earlier history described "context not found" as "the popup probably remains near the trigger element". That statement has been explicitly retracted. The checkpoints for static output are not near the trigger element, but the actual parent node under which Popup is created and the content area after the context lookup fails.

The static contract for Popup content fallback is: when the configured `content` cannot find context, create `body > .ui.popup` and place the content in `body > .ui.popup .content`.

This guidance only addresses the static fallback when context does not exist. It does not replace checks of display conditions, existing Popups, positioning results, or visual occlusion. If `body > .ui.popup` is observed during inspection, still confirm whether it is a node generated by this call; if that node is not observed during inspection, empty content alone is not enough to rule out the fallback either. First record separately whether context exists, the Popup parent node, and the content area, then decide where to stop.

The configured `content` is the input to verify here. It supplies the text content displayed in the Popup content area after creation. During inspection, do not treat the trigger element's `title`, text already on the page, or fields of other component objects as the same input source. If the content comes from another source, document the actual source first; this page only covers the relationship between the configured content and the fallback when context is not found.

## What to retain in the inspection record

The minimal record for the Popup branch can be very short, but it should make the sequence clear:

- Whether the context used by the call exists on the original page;
- Whether the Popup from this call appears on the page;
- The Popup's immediate parent node;
- Whether there is a content area in the Popup, and whether that area holds the configured content;
- Whether any nodes were added separately to reproduce the issue.

The minimal record for the Calendar branch should also have separate entries:

- The size classes actually present on the page;
- Whether the date table was generated;
- Selector observations for massive or mini;
- The behavior of `min-width` or any overrides affecting it.

Do not record "Popup works normally, Calendar works normally" as the only result. It does not indicate whether the inspection was performed on the original page or on a page that had already been temporarily patched, nor does it show at which layer the Calendar issue stops. Instead, if there is not enough evidence at a given step, explicitly writing "parent node not confirmed" or "date table not generated" is more useful than giving an overall judgment.

## Related issues not yet separated out

In the same batch of compatibility checks, whether this call reuses the Popup already on the page or creates one that coexists with it has not yet been organized into a separate rule. This affects the reliability of the observation "Popup found", but it is not Calendar Size Selector's issue. It is temporarily retained on this page to remind inspectors to distinguish the old node from the node for this call first; if a stable method for determining reuse emerges later, document it separately rather than putting it back into the context fallback branch.

Another unresolved item is call selection when multiple candidate contexts exist simultaneously. Existing material only requires confirming whether the passed-in object exists; an arbitrary similar node on the page cannot be treated as the matching target. If there is no pairing record for the call parameters and corresponding node, stop here.

## Old appendix: Temporary steps used in the past

The steps below are retained only for readers reviewing old troubleshooting records and must not be used as the current confirmation path:

1. Create a temporary node in the page with the same name as the expected context.
2. Trigger Popup again.
3. If the content is visible, label it as "possibly caused by a missing context".
4. If Calendar also became wider, it was recorded as "styles restored".

The third and fourth steps in this appendix were later overturned. The temporary node changed the page conditions and cannot prove the original fallback location; a wider Calendar also cannot prove that both the size selector and date table are correct. If this step was cited in old records, add the note "observed after manually changing the page" rather than deleting the result from that time.

Retaining the appendix also has a practical reason: early page screenshots often showed only the result "appeared after adding a node". We can now use this to know that it was a reproduction method, and will no longer mistakenly treat the screenshot as evidence of Popup's original mount location.

## 2025-04 Current troubleshooting entry

```text
Observed symptom
├─ Popup not in the expected area
│  ├─ Node found: record the direct parent node and content area
│  └─ Node not found: retain the context state and stop guessing the mount location
└─ Calendar dimensions differ
   ├─ Date table absent: stop at the rendering branch
   └─ Date table present: separately check the size classes and min-width source
```

When using this tree, Popup and Calendar must still have two separate observation records. Temporarily adding a context node changes the page conditions and can only be recorded separately as a reproduction experiment; it cannot override the result "node not found" on the original page.

## FUI-221 Theme interface clarification (quality-repair-022-v2-20260920)

The Calendar day table's `min-width` must come from an overridable theme width variable so that custom themes can change the compiled minimum width. Revision quality-repair-022-v2-20260920 clarifies that the public LESS interface is `@widthDay`, with a default of `18em`; invoke Fang Ke to override it in `src/site/modules/calendar.variables`, or override it via `modifyVars` when compiling LESS. Valid LESS length overrides (e.g. em, px, rem) should change the compiled `min-width` of `.ui.calendar .ui.table.day`; removing the override should restore the default, without restricting internal variable names or equivalent selector syntax.

This is an interface clarification for a later version of the task; earlier records only promised an overridable variable, so an earlier implementation must not be retroactively marked incorrect solely because it uses a different variable name.

# Decision Record: Modal Focus and Messages

When 2.9 was being wrapped up, autofocus after adding new inputs to Modal and Functional Validation Prompt Context were discussed in the same batch of issues, but that does not mean they should be treated as the same implementation problem. The former concerns where focus goes after Modal opens or its content changes; the latter concerns what context the caller can still access when validation rules return message text.

The earlier assessment was to start investigating on the Modal side when a new input did not receive focus as expected. The existing navigation points to `dist/components/modal.min.js`. That was just a convenient starting point for revisiting the issue at the time; it is not enough to attribute validation message semantics to Modal.

Two ways of documenting this were compared at the time.

- Record both symptoms as Modal compatibility issues, with one explanation covering both.
- Keep them separate: Modal only handles focus behavior after new focusable controls are added; continue investigating function-based messages through the form-validation calling context.

We chose the second option. Users encounter both issues in the same interaction, but the first concerns focus ownership and the second concerns the calling convention for message functions. Combining the descriptions would lead later readers to investigate "did not receive focus" as though the message function had not executed, and would also lead people changing validation messages to mistakenly think they need to change Modal.

We are not yet stating here that "a newly added input must always receive focus". We first need to confirm when the new control appears, whether existing focus should be retained, and whether a change in Modal content is the trigger. Without distinguishing these conditions, describing this as autofocus would overstate the actual behavior.

Function-based messages also remain an open investigation item for now. Message functions cannot be understood solely in terms of the rules for static text; we need to confirm what object is passed when they are called and what message users actually see after the call completes. No conclusion on this part is to be drawn from the Modal investigation entry point.

The decision is to retain two independent investigation trails: on the Modal trail, follow `dist/components/modal.min.js` to examine newly added inputs and focus; on the validation trail, examine context at the call sites for function-based messages. If the two trails do turn out to share a trigger, add a cross-reference then rather than retroactively merging the historical records.

# Modal Focus and Validation Prompt Decision Record

This record initially left behind only a highly misleading juxtaposition: autofocus after adding an input inside the Modal and the context of function-based validation prompts happened to be raised during the closeout of 2.9. To readers, they looked like the same compatibility chain, but in reality they started from different objects. The former starts with which control on the page owns focus after the Modal content changes; the latter starts with what invocation context the function runs in when the form validation executes the prompt function, and how the prompt text subsequently remains on the interface.

The initial draft did not try to find a common "root cause" for these two phenomena. That was not avoiding a decision, but avoiding turning a temporary search entry point into module ownership. Older investigation notes pointed the Modal issue name and call name to `dist/components/modal.min.js`; this made it the starting point for the focus issue, but cannot prove that the calling convention for function-based prompts is also defined there. A later review retained this distinction.

## Initial Tradeoffs

At the time, there were three ways to organize this.

First, merge them by user action: opening the Modal, dynamically adding an input, and triggering form validation would all be written up as one "popup form compatibility issue." This looked convenient, especially because, during reproduction, focus and prompts often appeared in succession. But it puts two judgments into the same result: as long as the new input is not focused, readers will suspect that the prompt function was never reached; as long as the prompt content does not match expectations, they may instead check the Modal focus code. Such a record is appealing for on-duty troubleshooting, but not helpful for subsequent changes.

Second, split it by file: everything navigable from `dist/components/modal.min.js` would be assigned to Modal, and all other content would go on a separate page. This option was not adopted either. Minified distribution files are suitable for confirming local entry points and adjacent calls, but not as the sole basis for dividing responsibility across components. In particular, the context of function-based prompts points to invocation of the validation rule itself, not to "who opened a Modal first."

Third, split them by behavioral object. The autofocus for the added input was retained as the focus issue following a Modal content change; Functional Validation Prompt Context was retained as the invocation issue for validation prompts. The two tracks can share one reproduction of the incident, while each clearly states what needs to be answered. The third option was adopted.

This decision has one direct cost: readers cannot get all the conclusions from a single title. The focus issue requires returning to Modal content changes and focus state; the prompt issue requires looking at the context the validation function receives when it is called, as well as how the error message is presented after the call completes. The cost is reasonable, because forcing them together would create a shared interface that does not exist.

## Old Assessment Retained on the Modal Side

The working assumption in the initial draft was simple: when the Modal is already displayed and a focusable input control is inserted only afterward, autofocus handling may still be limited to the moment of the initial display. This assumption explains the description "the actual entry point and sample result are inconsistent," but at the time it could not explain all variants.

The phrase "newly added inputs" here must not be silently broadened to cover arbitrary DOM changes. It involves at least three distinct points in time: inputs already present before the Modal is first shown; inputs created when the Modal is shown; inputs added only after the Modal has been shown. Collapsing all three into "the Modal automatically focuses inputs" would obscure whether focus actually comes from the initial scan, the display process, or subsequent change handling.

Another counterexample that must be retained is the case of existing focus. Even if a newly added control is focusable, that does not automatically mean it should take away the current focus. When a Modal already contains an element currently being edited, unconditionally focusing an input inserted later would instead alter the user's ongoing interaction. The initial draft more or less described "the new input is not focused" as a defect; after review, that statement is no longer sufficient. We first need to distinguish between "not updating the focus candidates" and "intentionally preserving existing focus".

Therefore, the current decision is not to state an absolute requirement in a single sentence, but to establish the questions to check for the Modal: whether content changes are observed; whether newly added focusable controls enter the candidate set; whether existing focus is preserved when present; whether, when there is no existing focus, a newly added input should become the target of the next autofocus. A single example cannot stand in for both of the last two branches here.

The related configuration name `observeChanges` remains a term to look out for during follow-up checks. Once observeChanges is enabled for the Modal, it observes content changes and updates autofocus behavior when new focusable controls are added. This statement explains the connection between content changes and autofocus, but it does not replace the branches described above: whether changes are observed and whether every change should take focus are two separate levels of judgment.

Earlier records treated this configuration as a single switch for "fixing newly added inputs", and that description is now retained as the historical position, no longer as an operational conclusion. It omitted whether newly added nodes are focusable, whether current focus can be preserved, and which kind of focus state is actually updated after observation occurs. Later reviews did not delete this passage, because it explains why the earliest examples framed the problem too narrowly.

## Decision on the Focus Issue

For the Modal track, the decision is as follows: record "autofocus for newly added inputs" as a focus ownership issue following content changes, rather than reducing it to an input element attribute issue.

There are two reasons for this wording. First, the issue is not whether the input tag itself includes the word autofocus, but whether focus selection reconsiders newly appearing focusable controls after the Modal has been displayed. Second, focus is part of the interaction state; if the page already has valid focus, any reselection may change keyboard interaction. Describing it merely as "adding autofocus" would obscure the compatibility cost.

The decision also explicitly rules out two approaches: do not use "new nodes always take priority" as the default rule, and do not use "nodes added after the initial display are always ignored" as the default rule. Both extremes prematurely turn unconfirmed judgments about timing into behavioral guarantees. The available material only supports placing the checks at the boundary between content observation and autofocus updates.

This is also why this issue still needs to be traced back through the Modal entry point, rather than getting sidetracked by the discussion of function-based validation messages. For FUI-206, the description when the card was created was that the actual entry point for adding inputs in Modal was inconsistent with the sample results. It is useful as a reference point for locating this behavior; it does not provide any conclusion about the message function's parameters.

## The validation-message track is now kept separate

Functional Validation Prompt Context was once included in the same section for a simple reason: users see the Modal first, then the validation error. This observation is not enough to establish that the same part of the implementation is responsible for both. The key to validation messages is not whether a dialog exists, but the context passed in when a rule calls the message function, and how the return value becomes a user-visible message.

The `prompt` in a form rule can provide failure message text, or a function that returns message text. The latter form should not be treated as syntactic sugar for the former. Static text only needs to be read on failure; the function-based form also requires the call site to determine its context. If this distinction is not documented, later readers can easily conflate the function returning error text with the function receiving the expected object.

The earlier, incorrect judgment was: as long as a message eventually appeared on the page, the context for the function-based message was correct. This judgment has been discarded. A message appearing on the page only shows that some message text entered the rendering flow, not that the message function necessarily ran in the expected context. Conversely, the function receiving the correct context is no substitute for checking what the user actually saw. Both checks need to be retained.

Therefore, the decision for the function-based message track is: do not infer its invocation semantics from the Modal focus behavior; record "how the function is called" and "how errors are displayed after the call" separately. For FUI-223, the record at creation was a review of the situation for Functional Validation Prompt Context, with a requirement to execute it as written in the help text and then confirm what the user can still see. This description supports retaining both stages of checks, but does not support inventing function parameters, return types, or specific error messages to fill in the gaps.

Another misreading should also be avoided here: the message function's context is not a detail worth checking only when an error occurs. It affects how the caller generates messages based on fields or rules. However, the current material does not provide the complete object used in the call or all rule types; this record does not expand them into a form API specification. For this closeout, it is sufficient to decide to separate it from the Modal focus issue, and require follow-up reviews to retain observations from both the calling side and the UI side.

## Why both tracks still need to be kept in one history

Separating them does not mean denying that they share a common scenario. Dynamically adding inputs in a Modal, then triggering validation, is one path that exposes both issues at once. The historical record needs to preserve this path, otherwise later readers will think the two topics were arbitrarily combined.

What the shared reproduction scenario can establish is sequence: content changes may affect focus first, and validation actions then produce messages. It cannot establish causality: focus failing to move does not automatically cause the message function's context to be incorrect, and incorrect message text does not automatically prove that content observation did not take effect. The initial draft was valuable for first documenting this juxtaposition; the update is valuable for making it explicit that juxtaposition is no longer treated as a causal explanation.

To ensure that this distinction went beyond wording, two independent sets of records were used in the subsequent review: the Modal side recorded only focus candidates, content changes, and the existing focus; the validation side recorded only message function calls and the final message. If both need to be reproduced together, the two sides can use the same page, but their outputs are still recorded separately. This prevents the example results from one side from overriding the conclusions on the other.

For maintainers, this boundary also offers a compatibility benefit. If Modal's content observation needs adjustment, the calling convention for validation messages should not be rewritten in the process; if the message function's context needs to be supplemented, Modal's existing focus rules should not be reset by default either. Scoping changes by object is more stable than scoping them by the original reproduction page.

## Facts and Gaps Retained After Review

The review did not turn the initial draft into a "resolved" record. What was actually added was the entry points to examine for each of the two tracks, along with where the earlier judgments were too strong.

The facts retained on the Modal side are: the issue is related to newly added focusable controls, content change observation, and autofocus updates; `observeChanges` is the searchable configuration name for this track. These facts support further examination of focus behavior, but do not imply that all dynamic nodes will immediately receive focus.

The facts retained on the validation side are: function-based `prompt` is not simply another way to write static message text; checks need to cover the context when the function is called, as well as the message that remains visible to the user after the call completes. These facts support further examination of the message function, but do not imply that it necessarily receives any object from Modal.

FUI-206 and FUI-223 serve only as navigation here. The former corresponds to the mismatch between the entry point for adding inputs and the example, while the latter corresponds to an inventory of the context for function-based messages in the reproduction scenario. Later status changes on the cards do not supersede this decision: a status can indicate that someone took on the work or compared approaches, but cannot replace an assessment of the focus and message behavior itself.

One gap remains unfilled: when Modal already has focus and a new input appears, the expected behavior needs to be confirmed against specific interaction scenarios. Another gap is whether function-based messages receive the same kind of context under different validation rules. Neither should be written up as an established fact just because the document has entered its finalization stage.

## Simplifications Rejected During Review

Someone once suggested reducing this record to a single sentence: "Update autofocus after a Modal mutation, and fix function-based messages at the same time." That sentence was not retained.

Its problem is not that it is insufficiently concise, but that it conflates two different verb-object pairs. "Update autofocus" describes focus selection; "fix function prompts" describes validation messaging.
