# Decision Record on Modal Focus and Validation Messages

Initially, this record preserved only an easily misleading juxtaposition: autofocus after adding an input in a Modal, and the context for function-based validation messages, both happened to come up during the wrap-up of 2.9. To readers, they looked like parts of the same compatibility path, but they actually started with different objects. The former starts with which control on the page has focus after the Modal content changes; the latter starts with the calling context in which a message function runs during form validation, and how the message text subsequently remains on screen.

The initial draft did not try to find a common "root cause" for these two behaviors. This was not an attempt to avoid a decision, but to avoid turning a temporary search entry point into a statement of module ownership. The old troubleshooting record pointed the issue and call names for Modal to `dist/components/modal.min.js`; this made it a starting point for the focus issue, but did not prove that the calling convention for function-based messages was also defined there. Subsequent review retained this distinction.

## The Initial Trade-off

There were three ways to organize the material on the table at the time.

The first was to combine everything by user workflow: opening a Modal, dynamically adding an input, and triggering form validation would all be documented as a single "modal form compatibility issue". This seemed convenient, especially because focus and messages often appeared in succession during reproduction. But it packed two judgments into the same outcome: whenever the new input was not selected, readers would suspect that execution had not reached the message function; whenever the message content did not meet expectations, they might instead go back and inspect the Modal focus code. This kind of record was appealing for troubleshooting during a shift, but did not help with later changes.

The second was to split the material by file: anything reachable from `dist/components/modal.min.js` would belong to Modal, and everything else would go on a separate page. This approach was not adopted either. Minified distribution files are useful for confirming local entry points and adjacent calls, but are not suitable as the sole basis for dividing responsibilities across components. In particular, the context for function-based messages is inherently a question about validation rule invocation, not about "who opened a Modal first".

The third was to split the material by the object of the behavior. Autofocus for newly added inputs would be retained as a focus issue following changes to Modal content; Functional Validation Prompt Context would be retained as an invocation issue for validation messages. The two tracks could share a single reproduction session, but each would clearly state the questions it needed to answer. The third approach was adopted.

This decision had one direct cost: readers could not get every conclusion from a single heading. The focus issue required returning to Modal content changes and focus state; the message issue required examining the context received by the validation function when invoked, and how error messages were presented after the call completed. That cost was reasonable, because forcing the two together would create a shared interface that did not exist.

## The Previous Assessment Retained on the Modal Side

The working hypothesis in the initial draft was straightforward: when a Modal was already displayed and a focusable input control was inserted afterward, autofocus handling might still be tied to the moment of the initial display. This hypothesis explained the description that "the actual entry point and the example produced different results", but at the time it could not explain every variant.

Here, "newly added inputs" must not be silently broadened to mean arbitrary DOM changes. This involves at least three distinct timing scenarios: inputs already exist before the Modal is first shown; inputs are created when the Modal is shown; inputs are added only after the Modal has already been shown. Conflating all three as "the Modal automatically focuses the input" obscures whether focus comes from the initial scan, the display process, or subsequent change handling.

Another counterexample that must be retained is existing focus. Even if a newly added control is focusable, that does not automatically mean it should steal the current focus. When a Modal already contains an element being edited, unconditionally focusing an input inserted later would instead change the user's ongoing interaction. The initial draft more or less described "the new input is not focused" as a defect; after review, that description is no longer sufficient. We first need to distinguish between "focus candidates were not updated" and "existing focus was deliberately preserved".

Therefore, the current decision is not to issue a single absolute requirement, but to establish the questions to check for Modal: whether content changes are observed; whether newly added focusable controls enter the candidate set; whether existing focus, if any, is preserved; and, when there is no existing focus, whether the newly added input should become the target of the next autofocus. A single example cannot be used to substitute one of these final two branches for the other.

The related configuration name `observeChanges` remains a term to watch for when revisiting this issue. When observeChanges is enabled for a Modal, it observes content changes and updates autofocus behavior when focusable controls are added. This statement establishes a connection between content changes and autofocus, but it does not replace the branches described above: whether changes are observed and whether every change should steal focus are judgments at two different levels.

Earlier records treated this configuration as a single switch to "fix newly added inputs". That wording is now retained as a record of the earlier position and no longer serves as an operational conclusion. It omitted whether newly added nodes are focusable, whether the current focus can be preserved, and what type of focus state is actually updated after observation occurs. The later review did not delete this passage because it explains why the earliest examples framed the issue too narrowly.

## Decision on the Focus Issue

For the Modal workstream, the decision is as follows: record "autofocus for newly added inputs" as a focus ownership issue following content changes, rather than reducing it to an attribute issue for an input element.

There are two reasons for this wording. First, the issue is not whether the input tag itself contains autofocus, but whether focus selection reconsiders newly appearing focusable controls after the Modal has been shown. Second, focus is part of the interaction state; if the page already has valid focus, any reselection may change keyboard interaction. Describing it merely as "adding autofocus" would obscure the compatibility cost.

The decision also explicitly rules out two approaches: neither "new nodes always take priority" nor "nodes added after the initial display are always ignored" is to be the default rule. Both extremes prematurely turn unconfirmed timing judgments into behavioral guarantees. The available material only supports placing the check at the boundary between content observation and autofocus updates.

This is also why the issue still needs to be traced back from the Modal entry point, rather than being diverted into a discussion of functional validation messages. For FUI-206, the card's creation-time description said that the actual entry point for adding an input in Modal did not match the sample result. It is suitable as a navigation point for this phenomenon; it does not provide a conclusion about the validation-message function's parameters.

## Validation-prompt thread no longer to be merged

Functional Validation Prompt Context was once placed in the same section for a simple reason: users would see Modal first, then the validation error. This observation is insufficient to show that the two have the same implementation responsibilities. The key to validation messages is not whether the pop-up exists, but the context supplied when the rule calls the validation-message function and how the return value becomes a user-visible message.

A form rule's `prompt` can provide failure-message text, or a function that returns message text. The latter form should not be treated as syntactic sugar for the former. Static text only needs to be read when validation fails; the functional form also requires the call site to determine its context. If this distinction is not written down, later readers may easily conflate the function returning the wrong text with the function receiving the expected object.

An earlier incorrect judgment was: as long as a message ultimately appeared on the page, the functional message context was correct. This judgment has been discarded. A message on the page only shows that some message text entered the rendering process; it cannot by itself show that the validation-message function ran in the expected context. Conversely, receiving the correct context in the function cannot replace checking what the user actually saw. Both need to be retained.

Therefore, the decision for the functional validation-message thread is: do not infer its call semantics from Modal's focus behavior; record separately how the function is called and how the error is rendered after the call. For FUI-223, the creation record contains Functional Validation Prompt Context's on-site inventory, and requires executing it as written in the help text and then confirming what users can still see. This description supports retaining two checks, but not fabricating function parameters, return types, or specific error wording in its place.

Another misreading should also be avoided here: the context of the validation-message function is not a detail worth checking only when an error occurs. It affects how the caller generates messages based on fields or rules. However, the current material does not provide the complete call object, nor all rule types; this record does not expand them into a form API specification. For this closeout, the sufficient decision is to separate it from the Modal focus issue and require subsequent review to retain observations from both the caller side and the UI side.

## Why the two threads should still remain in one history

Separating them does not mean denying that they share the same incident context. Adding an input dynamically in Modal and then triggering validation is one path that exposes both issues at the same time. The historical record needs to preserve this path; otherwise, people later will think the two topics were arbitrarily combined.

The shared reproduction scenario can establish a sequence: content changes may affect focus first, and validation actions then produce messages. It cannot establish causality: focus not moving does not automatically cause the message function's context to be wrong, nor does incorrect message text automatically prove that content observation did not take effect. The initial draft's value was in first documenting these observations side by side; the updated version's value is in making clear that their coexistence is no longer treated as a causal explanation.

To ensure this distinction was more than a matter of wording, subsequent review used two independent sets of records: the Modal records included only focus candidates, content changes, and existing focus; the validation records included only message function calls and the final messages. If the scenario requires reproducing both at the same time, both sides can use the same page, but their outputs are still recorded separately. This prevents sample results on one side from overriding conclusions on the other.

For maintainers, this boundary also offers a compatibility benefit. If Modal's content observation needs adjustment, the calling convention for validation messages should not be rewritten in passing; if the message function's context needs to be supplemented, Modal's existing focus rules should not be reset by default either. Dividing the scope of changes by the object involved is more stable than dividing it by the original reproduction page.

## Facts and gaps retained after review

The review did not turn the initial draft into a record marked "resolved". What was actually added was the entry points to inspect for each of the two tracks, along with an account of where the earlier judgments had been too strong.

The facts retained on the Modal side are: the issue is related to newly added focusable controls, observation of content changes, and autofocus updates; `observeChanges` is the searchable configuration name for this track. These facts support further inspection of focus behavior, but do not imply that all dynamic nodes will immediately receive focus.

The facts retained on the validation side are: function-based `prompt` is not simply another way to write static message text; inspection must cover the context when the function is called, as well as the message that remains visible to the user after the call completes. These facts support further inspection of the message function, but do not imply that it necessarily obtains any object from Modal.

FUI-206 and FUI-223 serve only as navigation here. The former corresponds to the mismatch between the entry point for adding inputs and the example, while the latter corresponds to taking stock of the context for function-based messages in the reproduction scenario. Subsequent status changes on the cards do not replace this decision: statuses can indicate that the work was picked up or that alternatives were compared, but they cannot replace an assessment of focus and message behavior themselves.

One gap still has not been filled: when Modal already has focus and a new input appears, the expected behavior needs to be confirmed against a specific interaction scenario. Another gap is whether function-based messages receive the same kind of context under different validation rules. Neither should be written up as an established fact simply because the document has already entered the wrap-up stage.

## Simplified wording rejected during review

Someone once suggested reducing this record to a single sentence: "Update autofocus after Modal mutation, and fix function-based messages at the same time." This sentence was not retained.

The problem is not that it is not concise enough, but that it conflates two different verb–object pairs. "Update autofocus" describes focus selection; "fix function-based messages" describes validation messages. The first half does not explain how existing focus is handled, and the second half does not explain whether the problem lies in the function context or the rendered result. Using this sentence as a change description is likely to lead to unrelated changes across modules.

Moving all the details to DOC-16 and leaving only a link here was also considered. This was not adopted. DOC-16 discusses focus ownership in Modal mutation and the two-layer boundary of novalidate; it can help explain related focus issues, but cannot replace the separate treatment of function-based message context in this requirements history. What needs to remain here is why these two topics were once grouped together and why they were later separated, rather than a copy of the discussion from another document.

The last rejected approach was to judge whether both tracks were working correctly solely from a screenshot of the final UI. A screenshot is useful for confirming whether the user sees a message, but is insufficient for determining when focus changes or how the message function is called. It can only capture part of the scenario, not serve as the sole criterion.

## Current decisions

The following decisions remain in place:

1. Handle autofocus after new inputs are added to a Modal according to focus ownership after content changes, focusing checks on the relationship among newly added focusable controls, content observation, and existing focus.
2. Treat Functional Validation Prompt Context as an issue with the invocation of form validation messages, checking the function call context and the message the user ultimately sees, rather than drawing conclusions about it from the Modal entry point.
3. The two tracks may share a reproduction page, but their records and changes must remain separate; an example for one track cannot establish the behavior of the other.
4. `dist/components/modal.min.js` continues to serve as a local navigation entry point for the Modal track. Verification of function-based messages should continue at the validation call sites, rather than being assigned to this file by default because it is part of the same batch of requirements.
5. The initial draft's rough judgments that "a new input not receiving focus is a defect" and "the presence of a message means the function context is correct" are both retained as historical judgments that have since been narrowed, not as current conclusions.

These decisions do not turn the issues into two disconnected islands. They retain the shared scenario and acknowledge that the two behaviors can occur one after another in the same interaction; however, each track's attribution, checks, and scope of changes must stand on their own.

## Reading order for handoff

If a newly added input does not receive the expected focus, start with the Modal's content changes and the current focus state, and do not change the message function first. If the focus selection has already been confirmed to match expectations, then check which timing is still missing between the entry point and example indicated by FUI-206.

If functional validation messages do not behave as expected, first distinguish whether the issue is with the function-call context or with how the function result is rendered after it reaches the page. FUI-223 preserves the navigation for this evidence inventory. Do not use "happens in the same Modal" as a substitute for these two branches.

If the investigation also involves focus ownership for Modal mutation or the form's novalidate boundary, then turn to DOC-16. That material addresses an adjacent boundary; the conclusion of this record remains that autofocus for newly added inputs and Functional Validation Prompt Context are listed side by side in the change history but should be evaluated separately.

## Evidence Still to Be Added

- Record a case where an element already has focus and a focusable input is then added, and confirm whether focus should be retained.
- Record a case with no focusable target initially, where an input is added after the content changes, and confirm the timing of the autofocus update.
- Record the context available when functional `prompt` is called, and save it separately from the message text in the final UI.

## Decision Status Quick Reference

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2

    Keep previous description --> Current review: Date and current entry point listed side by side

```

The state diagram only summarizes the evolution of this decision record; it does not fill in implementation conclusions that have not yet been obtained.

## 2.9 Final determination (2026-09-26, currently authoritative)

The focus rules for newly added inputs are determined by FUI-206/FUI-210's current owner, core-03; guesses in the old record recommending that focus be retained on the old input or that actions be performed only on the active modal are no longer current requirements. # Modal Focus Boundary Trial Proposal

This proposal retains the two original questions: after a content mutation in a visible Modal, is a newly added control's autofocus allowed to change focus; and when novalidate is present, at which layer do browser-native validation and form module validation each stop? The previous version treated both as isolated switches. Review later showed that this conflated two different ownership questions.

The old recommendation remains here: reprocess autofocus whenever a focusable control is added to the content area. This works for a minimal fixture, but should not go straight into the default behavior. It did not distinguish three situations: an active control already exists inside the Modal, the caller has just moved focus to an element, or the new node simply comes later in the render order. Stealing focus in the first case would interrupt form input; overriding it in the second would prevent the caller from maintaining its own interaction; in the third, a node should not gain priority simply because it has appeared.

The candidate approaches listed at the time were:

- **Prioritize new nodes.** Scan focusable nodes after a mutation and let a node with autofocus take over. This requires the least implementation logic, but treats existing focus as meaningless.
- **Prioritize the initial display.** Process autofocus only when the Modal is shown; subsequent mutations only update content. This is conservative, but dynamically inserted input controls get no chance to receive the expected focus.
- **Preserve existing ownership.** Allow autofocus to be checked again after a mutation, but move focus only when there is no active control inside the Modal, or the caller has not explicitly set focus. This approach requires the fixture to record whether focus was set before the mutation, after it, or through external interaction; looking only at the final DOM is not enough.

The proposal leaned toward the third approach at the time, not because it had been proven correct, but because it separated "a new control exists" from "focus should change." The same Modal needs to contain an existing input, an input inserted later, and an input inserted later with autofocus; compare only the active element before and after the mutation. `dist/components/modal.min.js` is a nearby entry point for this inspection, where it should be possible to confirm whether mutation observation and autofocus handling are still connected. This proposal should not be rewritten as an implementation description until an environment where the fixture can be modified is available.

The old statement about novalidate also needs to be narrowed. The previous version equated the attribute's presence with "no validation." That only described what the test intended to verify; it did not establish whether the browser's native validity checks and the module's validation command share the same decision logic. The "two layers" here should first be split into two questions: does submission still trigger browser-side constraint checks; and when `validate form` is called explicitly, does the form module still perform the validation described by fields, rules, and prompt? The answers may be the same or different. Until the fixture separates the entry points, novalidate alone cannot establish the second answer.

The boundary to try is: keep the same fields configuration, first observe whether native validation messages appear through the submission path, then call `validate form` on its own. If the module call still produces a result, record which set of rules produced it rather than attributing it to the browser ignoring novalidate. If the module call no longer produces a result, also confirm whether that is caused by the attribute branch or by the fixture not entering the original form initialization path. No new rules are required here; only keep both entry points available independently.

After the interface review, the focus portion was moved into the follow-up checks in FUI-207; permission to modify the fixture was also handed over as testing moved to the next stage. Routine novalidate checks were added to FUI-224. The two cards retain only the execution entry points; this older record remains the reference for the proposal's trade-offs.

The withdrawal conditions have not changed either: withdraw "prioritize new nodes" if a later-inserted node overrides existing focus inside the Modal without user action; withdraw the statement "attribute present means no validation" if the fixture proves that the novalidate submission path and explicit module validation are independent branches. No results from a new round are attached here, so the third focus approach and the split into two entry points remain trial recommendations from that time, not an ongoing compatibility commitment.

Both surfaced in the same compatibility cleanup, but there is not enough evidence to treat them as the same state issue.

Two approaches were compared at the time. One was to make the cache setting a global switch and address focus through the same interaction fix; the other was to retain the existing remote query configuration, provide a bypass for just that request, and investigate focus separately. The latter was chosen. A global change would affect queries with no reported issues, and the cache lead did not explain focus ownership after using the remove icon.

The source review started at `src/definitions/modules/dropdown.js`. `preSelected`, `menuConfig`, and `value` all appear near initialization in that file and serve as starting points for inspecting remote queries; this does not establish that Search's focus issue belongs to dropdown.

It remains undecided whether the input, results area, or another element should receive focus after using the remove icon. Keep this as a separate issue rather than settling it as an implementation detail alongside cache bypass.

versions.body:
# Cache Bypass and Focus Decision Record

The initial draft put "One-Time Remote Cache Bypass" and "Search remove icon Focus" on the same page because both reports were part of the compatibility review for 2.9. That write-up separated their scopes, but did not record why a unified fix was not chosen at the time, or distinguish between "query results did not update as expected" and "focus was in the wrong place after an interaction". Later, anyone following the titles to find the code could easily end up tracing the second issue into dropdown as well.

This addendum retains the conclusion from May: the two issues will not be combined into a single state change. The cache track concerns whether a particular remote query should ignore stored results; the focus track concerns where keyboard input should continue to be received after a remove icon operation ends. The former can involve a one-time intent, while the latter requires first confirming the specific triggering element and focus target. Calling both issues "inconsistent interaction" is not sufficient justification for a shared implementation.

The options compared in May have not been deleted and are retained here as they were:

- **Make caching a single shared toggle.** This would make the observed differences easiest to explain, but would extend the need for a single query to other remote queries. This approach was not adopted.
- **Treat remove icon as a side effect of the same toggle.** No observations at the time showed that the focus changes came from cache reads or cache bypass, so this approach was not adopted.
- **Specify the files to modify based solely on issue names.** The earlier investigation did bring the terms query, module, dropdown, clear, cache, and api into the dropdown module; however, a name match does not mean that both behaviors are handled by the same event code. This approach was not adopted as a decision either.
- **Keep two independent entry points.** For remote queries, inspect dropdown first; for remove icon, continue looking for the actual focus chain. This scope split was adopted.

The decision at the time was not to disable caching permanently, nor was it a promise that every query would bypass existing results. It covered only the limited intent of a "one-time bypass": if a later implementation does provide this entry point, it should not be interpreted as a global configuration migration. This preserves the meaning of the existing query configuration and avoids having callers change the entire remote-result handling process to an uncached path because of one observed inconsistency.

The initial draft contained an overly optimistic judgment: "Since the path already leads to dropdown, the focus issue can probably be handled along the way." This sentence is now marked **no longer applicable**. It was not a finding from reproducing the issue, but merely placed the titles of two issues being wrapped up in the same round too close together. The September review did not uncover a call relationship linking remove icon to remote caching, so this statement should no longer be used to sequence implementation work.

## Retained Code Annotations

The current starting point for inspecting the query side is `src/definitions/modules/dropdown.js`. The file begins with:

```js
function isFunction(obj) {
```

It is at line 14 and is one of the module's existing local utilities. It does not explain the caching strategy, but can help distinguish configuration values from callback values when inspecting conditional branches.

The other recorded locations are also only nearby points: at line 566, `$subMenu` gets the menu from `selector.menu`; line 773 saves `$input.val()` to `preSelected`; line 836 creates `menuConfig`; `value` appears at line 843; line 945 contains `$lastDivider`; line 1712 retains the `events` binding. These names show that the file handles menus, selected values, and event organization, which is enough to make it a starting point for investigating remote queries. They do not answer the question of the focus target for Search remove icon Focus.

The main outcome of this review was to narrow the earlier implications. The previous record linked `$subMenu`, `preSelected`, and `events` into a narrative of "possibly restoring focus after caching"; now, only their individual locations are retained. Without an actual event sequence, variable names cannot be assembled into a behavioral path. In particular, `preSelected` only shows that the input value was read here, and does not support an inference about whether the input is refocused after the remove icon action.

## Boundaries of the Cache Track

Remote queries and result caching are already part of the dropdown module's context, so it is reasonable to continue starting the query-side investigation from this file. What must be avoided is incorrectly recording "bypass once" as "change the caching policy". The two requirements concern different things: the former is about whether a single request can obtain fresh results, while the latter is about whether subsequent queries generally use the cache. In May, the former wording was retained because the reported scenario supported only one-time handling, with no material supporting a global reversal of behavior.

There was also discussion at the time about putting the bypass action in the caller and having the caller attach a temporary marker. This option was not retained as a formal decision, not because it was necessarily impossible to implement, but because it would leave each caller to interpret the boundary of "next" independently: the next input, the next remote request, or the next menu opening. Without a consistent trigger boundary, the temporary actions implemented by callers would differ. The record therefore only requires confirming the module's existing query entry point first, then deciding where the marker should go.

"Preserving configuration" here is also not an assertion about any particular field or specific API. The initial draft did not record an executable interface, call parameters, or test output; this review likewise has not invented those details from variable names. What it retains is a narrower design judgment: a one-time need should not default to a global change. If the actual entry point is found later, this must still be reassessed based on that entry point's lifecycle.

Another abandoned claim was that "a cache hit will definitely prevent focus from returning to the input". This was used as a convenient explanation in the May discussion draft, but was not retained. A cache hit describes how results are obtained, while focus describes ownership of DOM after an interaction ends; the two may occur in sequence during the same user operation, but neither can be treated as the cause of the other based on sequence alone.

## The Focus Track Was Not Closed at the Same Time

The Search remove icon issue remains open for investigation into the effects of input and the environment. The available material provides only the issue name, not the element that held focus before the click, the result state after removal, whether keyboard operations were involved, or the expected focus target. Given these gaps, no implementation decision such as "always return to the input field" was made in May, nor was there a decision to let the menu or results area take over focus.

This is not avoiding a decision. What has been decided is that cache bypass cannot be used to explain focus ownership, and the focus issue cannot justify changing remote caching behavior. What has not been decided is who should receive focus when the remove icon operation ends. Separating the decided boundaries from the unconfirmed target allows later checks to avoid inventing nonexistent causality just to make the two records look consistent.

After the September review, the order of investigation for the focus track also changed. First reconstruct the actual remove icon operation in the report, then record the focus nodes before and after removal; only after confirming that this node chain passes through dropdown's event bindings should the investigation return to the area around line 1712. If the focus chain does not enter this module, the cache decision should no longer be treated as background for this issue. This sequence replaces the initial draft's instruction to "first look for a shared fix point in the query module".

## Corrections to the Earlier Judgments on This Page

The valuable part of the initial draft was its scope split, not the code ownership it implied. It correctly prevented handling the issue through a global cache toggle, and correctly kept the focus issue separate; its less accurate part was presenting the same file path as though it were common evidence for both issues.

The following earlier position is therefore retained but no longer followed:

> dropdown is the shared modification location for these two issues, so changing the cache branch first will also produce the focus fix.

That position was later overturned. The current review confirms only that the dropdown file contains local declarations related to queries, menus, and values, along with adjacent event code; it does not confirm that the file also handles the focus changes for Search remove icon. Future references to this page should treat it as a history of the decisions at the time, not as a conclusion locating the code responsible for the focus issue.

Another earlier constraint that must also be retained is that no evidence was recorded to support "immediately switching to globally uncached behavior". Even if a new caller later reports a similar scenario, the limited decision from May cannot be directly expanded into a global policy. First distinguish whether the superficially similar result is caused by result caching, request timing, the displayed selected value, or focus transfer.

## Points Still Open for Investigation

- Inspect the area around `preSelected` to confirm which part of value handling it participates in, and avoid incorrectly recording an input-value read as cache state.
- Inspect the areas around `menuConfig` and `value` to confirm whether query configuration and menu rendering appear in the same branch.
- Near `events`, trace only actions actually bound to remove icon; if there is no such binding, stop keeping the focus issue on this file path.
- Clarify the counting unit of "next" for a one-time bypass before deciding whether module-internal state is needed.

This page has not added implementation steps, nor has it presented an unconfirmed focus target as a compatibility commitment. The retained decisions are narrow: investigate One-Time Remote Cache Bypass as a single-query intent; investigate Search remove icon Focus as an independent interaction; the two tracks do not share a rationale for a fix until an actual event chain is available.

## Decision Flow at the Time

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> LocalBypassProposal
    LocalBypassProposal --> SeparateInvestigation: Caching and focus do not share a rationale
    SeparateInvestigation --> PendingConfirmation: Next query and focus event chain
```

The states here correspond only to the decisions recorded on this page, and do not indicate that the two implementation paths have already been merged.

# Modal and Dropdown Interface Proposal

The initial draft put Multi Modal Inner dimmer and Dropdown Custom data Attributes together, for a simple reason: both fall near the compatibility closeout around 2.9, and both can easily cause additional page changes through a single local change. The arrangement at the time was to inspect the Modal side using `src/definitions/modules/modal.js` first, then attach the Dropdown observations to the same round of material. This arrangement has been retained, but the implicit judgment that "they can be closed out together" needs to be removed.

The commonality between the two objects extends only to the timing of observation. Both should record the state before the call, then check after the call what was added to the page, removed, or remained unchanged. Beyond this, what they evaluate differs: the inner dimmer is the visible state after stacking, while Dropdown concerns whether attached data produces a visible result. Putting them into one combined sample makes it difficult to tell which side invalidated the conclusion when it fails.

One working assumption in the initial draft was: as long as the Modal stacking sample is stable, the Dropdown observation from the same round can be treated as part of the compatibility closeout. This statement is no longer being adopted. A stable Modal sample cannot establish how custom data is handled; conversely, a visible change in Dropdown cannot show that the dimmer in multiple Modal layers is in the correct state. The two types of result can be stored side by side, but they cannot replace each other.

## Adjustments from Existing Material

FUI-212 first entered release-related processing, then moved into the actual processing phase. The local requirement left by that card is to save Multi Modal Inner dimmer's visible results separately for one successful call and one failed call. This requirement makes the Modal side's trial goal very specific: it is not an abstract confirmation that "multiple Modals are supported", but enabling later viewers to see the difference in stacking results between the two calls.

Therefore, the minimum unit of a Modal sample is a pair of comparable calls, not a single screenshot or a single status statement. Each side should retain the visible Modals already present before the call, the position or state of the visible dimmer, and the page's layering result after the subsequent call. No particular DOM structure is assumed here, nor is the node count at a particular moment treated as a complete conclusion; the card calls for a difference users can see, and the material should first reconstruct that difference.

One reproduction was later completed for FUI-229. The entry point for this object requires reproducing Dropdown Custom data Attributes starting from the pre-call state and confirming whether any additional visible change remains after completion. The subsequent addendum still leaves one item unconfirmed. This means the Dropdown side can only record results already seen and unconfirmed points; it cannot fill in attribute names, normalization rules, or final presentation just to make the two tracks end at the same time.

The timeline of the two cards also does not support collapsing them into a single completion criterion. FUI-212 already has an independent observation track with a success/failure comparison; FUI-229 still has unconfirmed parts. If both are required to pass together, the Dropdown unknowns will obscure Modal differences that are already ready for further work, while the visible Modal result will in turn be misread as corroborating evidence for data-attribute handling.

## Modal-Side Trial Track

Keep `src/definitions/modules/modal.js` as the reading and historical cross-check entry point for the Modal side. It can help review existing module relationships around the multi-Modal issue, but the current material does not assign Dropdown's attribute handling to this file. During the trial, do not describe this path as a shared fix point, nor use it to assign implementation ownership for the other object.

For a successful call, the record should answer three local questions: which Modals were already displayed before the call; what visible state the dimmer already on the page was in; and what happened to the visible state related to the previous layer after the subsequent Modal appeared. If the result is merely "the UI is normal", it cannot later be compared with the failed call. Conversely, if it can state that a layer remained visible, changed, or did not change as expected, the sample has reviewable content.

For a failed call, the record likewise starts from the pre-call state. Failure is not a sufficient description of the phenomenon; the post-call stacking result must be retained, and the visible stage at which it differs from the successful sample must be identified. If the starting points differ, for example, if the states of the originally displayed Modals differ, mark that difference first rather than rushing to attribute the result to the inner dimmer. Such a record still has value, but it can only serve as a clue, not replace a comparable pair of samples.

This round does not recommend using "any number of Modals can display normally" to describe the pass condition. The current material only requires retaining the results of one successful call and one failed call; it provides no range that can be extrapolated to all stacking configurations. The trial material should maintain this boundary: it serves to review the visible results of these two calls, not to expand a local observation into a general guarantee.

When the successful and failed calls can be reconstructed from comparable starting points, the work represented by FUI-212 can proceed, even if the Dropdown concern remains unresolved. Conversely, if the two calls cannot be compared from similar starting points, pause using them for the stacking assessment, retain the existing page results and the explanation of their differences, and wait for a sample that can reconstruct the starting point. What is paused is this pair of comparisons, not an overall judgment of the Modal module's existing behavior.

## Dropdown-Side Trial Track

The records for FUI-229 begin with the pre-call state, not with the page's final text. They should record whether the value object carries custom data, the relevant content already on the page before the call, and whether any additional visible change occurs after completion. Here, "additional visible change" is an observation question, not a pre-specified behavior. The material provides no attribute mapping or rendering form that can be hard-coded, so a result cannot be set in advance and the reproduction process then written as confirmation of it.

Changes in the value text and visible changes from attached data must be written separately. If only text presentation was confirmed after the call, record only text presentation; if an additional change was seen but it still cannot be determined whether it came from data, retain that uncertainty as well. Writing either situation as "custom data handling is complete" would exceed the currently known scope. The addendum to FUI-229 has explicitly left one item unconfirmed; the trial track should carry this gap into the subsequent review rather than fill it with the Modal result.

Subsequent Dropdown samples also do not need to use `src/definitions/modules/modal.js` as a locating reference. That path is practically useful for historical verification of the inner dimmer, but it has not established a relationship between data-attribute handling and the Modal file. If a clear entry point specific to Dropdown is obtained later, it can then be connected to the observation records of FUI-229; until then, the before-and-after call states remain this track's only reliable basis for comparison.

The stopping point on this side is more direct than for Modal: once it cannot be confirmed whether the additional change is related to data, stop assigning a cause, leaving the pre-call state, the page result already seen, and the unconfirmed items. Do not fill in attributes that "should appear", and do not use an unrelated stacking sample to prove that it has passed. Although this will not produce a neat conclusion, it preserves the point where the next reproduction genuinely needs to pick up.

## Merge Approaches Not Adopted

The first discarded approach is to create a combined regression with "both issues succeeding simultaneously". It appears to reduce the number of samples, but in practice mixes the sources of failure: when the stacking state is abnormal, the Dropdown change may be impossible to assess; when the data attribute still has an open question, the observed dimmer difference is dragged into an overall failure. An overall presentation can be done later, but it cannot replace two local records.

The second discarded approach is to treat the Modal file path as the shared implementation entry point for both issues. The existing path provides navigation only for reading and historical cross-checking of multiple Modals; no material says that Dropdown attribute handling belongs in the same place. Continuing to use this wording would expand a real check starting point into an unconfirmed ownership judgment.

The third discarded approach is to define in advance what extra change must appear after Dropdown is complete. FUI-229 only require reproducing from the pre-call state and confirming whether a change remains; they provide no specific behavior that can be fixed in advance. A preset result would turn observation into a search for traces supporting it, so it cannot serve as the basis for this trial.

The fourth discarded approach is to stop all further organization of FUI-212 because FUI-229 still has unconfirmed items. The two work items are adjacent within the same compatibility closeout round, but their user-visible risks are not the same. FUI-212 has an independent success/failure comparison requirement; as long as the sample starting points are comparable, there is no reason for the other object's unknowns to automatically cancel this observation track.

## Current Arrangement

Retain two independent sets of material. FUI-212 should record the visible stacking results of the inner dimmer for successful and failed calls, and pause attribution when starting points cannot be compared. FUI-229 should continue verifying from before-and-after call states whether custom data attributes leave an additional visible change; when the source cannot be confirmed, retain the uncertainty and do not write it as complete.

The two sets of material can be reviewed in the same round and can share page-level background records, but they do not share a pass conclusion. When revisiting Modal, start from `src/definitions/modules/modal.js`; when continuing to verify Dropdown, return to the call scenario of FUI-229. This split does not promise that the two objects will be completely unrelated from now on; it merely refuses, before their relationship has been established, to use one side's sample result to close out the other side's issue.

# Inline popup content troubleshooting tree

When a popup has appeared but the text source looks wrong, or when a tooltip's position and wait time are wrong the first time it appears, first separate the two symptoms. Don't change them together in the same initialization block just because both occur next to the trigger element.

## Inline popup content

Start reproducing with the inline popup already present on the trigger element. First note whether the existing node is still on the page, what text is actually visible, and whether initialization provided content; at this step, don't add a title first, and don't delete and rebuild the existing node.

- If the existing inline popup is still being reused, check whether content is an available source for this display. The existing inline popup should not be replaced by the trigger element's title; title is only a fallback when no other content source exists.
- If the original node was not reused, stop at the popup creation point and confirm whether the issue is node selection or content source. Don't directly classify "wrong text" as a delayed-style issue.
- If it only reproduces when title is present, retain the minimal snippet of the trigger element and initialization configuration; record the case without content separately from the case with an existing inline node.

When tracing to the runtime entry point, start looking at the locations adjacent to `inline`, `popup`, and `title` in `dist/components/popup.min.js`. Adjacent literals in the minified file are not enough to establish content precedence; base the determination on the node retained during reproduction.

## Tooltip's first display

Check this branch only for elements with `data-tooltip` and no position set. The style target should be `[data-tooltip]:not([data-position])::after`; first confirm that the page matches this pseudo-element rather than another set of rules after a position attribute has been applied.

If the selector matches, check two things: the delay is controlled by `transition-delay`, and the initial transform should be `translateX(-50%) scale(0.8)`. If the former is missing, it will start too early; if the latter is inconsistent, the first display will not be centered or in the expected scale state. The path is still retained because some old regression records left only this reference; it points to `internal/FUI`'s `v_prev`, not a description that can stand in for the current release's behavior.

The working assumption in the old records has not been removed: a cache hit takes a separate callback route, while normal queries only fill in results. This was a judgment written down at the time to narrow the search scope. During a later review, what could be observed consistently was the adjacency of Query and Results Pipeline, and one cache callback marker location was still unconfirmed; "separate route" can therefore no longer be treated as a migration premise.
```
Old investigation: issue name ──> call name ──> cache in search.min.js

Migration check: release-build runtime context ──> parameter order ──> actual returned status
                              │

```

Here, order means the sequence of values the caller passes to Search, not their textual positions in the minified file. Old records often conflated the two: the fact that `query` and `cache` are close together in the artifact does not mean the caller has already triggered them with the same set of parameters.

Next, record just two observations: whether the call enters Search; what status it returns when the call ends. The second must come from runtime observation, not from whether a title appears on the page. Investigations of the old version once treated the presence of a title as query completion, but this was later shown to be insufficient to establish that the cache callback had left a marker. `title` can help confirm that the result object is still on the result side, but cannot support a conclusion about caching on its own.

`dist/components/search.min.js` is suitable for the following two tasks.

- Locate the adjacent names `query`, `search`, `onresults`, `cache`, `response`, `title` in the old-version compatibility records, to confirm that the starting point recorded at the time did not specify the wrong file.

# Search Results Styling Decision Record

When this decision was first recorded, "Customizable Search Result Styling" was described as a standalone visual requirement: the panel should not be rigidly constrained when there are many results, nor leave unsightly blank space when there are few. This wording identified the size of the results area as something worth addressing, but did not provide consistent page conditions. It was not enough to determine whether to change the theme, change the search module, or simply add an override to a particular page using it.

The initial draft did not commit to fixed dimensions or specify the minified file as the only implementation location. This remains unchanged. The search component, the results container, and the pages using the search component are not the same thing; combining them in a single styling fix can easily lead to page-local rules being mistaken for component-level behavior.

The initial draft's decision was to leave room for resizing in the results area. Looking back, that phrase actually conflated three things: whether the results area has a height cap, which direction users can resize it in, and whether the result content remains within the original scrollable area after resizing. The first is a style constraint, the second is a permitted interaction direction, and only the third concerns how the result content is contained. They can no longer be represented by the single phrase "the panel is resizable".

## Trade-offs from the Initial Draft

A fixed height was one candidate. Its advantages were that screenshots would be easy to compare and it would not add any post-drag states; the problem was that it put long and short lists into the same box. A consistent appearance does not establish that the original usable space remains available, especially for scrollable results areas: an unchanged panel does not mean users can still see or interact with more results. A fixed height is therefore not adopted as the default approach.

Another candidate was to attribute the issue directly to theme variables. This would appear to keep changes small and make it easy to explain as a skin difference. But although themes can affect width, spacing, and visual hierarchy, that does not justify reducing "whether resizing is allowed, in which direction, and whether to remove the height cap" to theme choices. The existing material does not support that classification, so theme variables are not the implementation target for this decision.

Adding an override only on the consuming page was also an option. It is the most direct approach for a single page and has a limited scope of impact; the cost is that the same search results would follow different sizing rules on different pages. The initial draft established no page-specific exceptions, so a page-level patch cannot be used first in place of an assessment at the component level. This option is reserved for pages where a layout exception can later be confirmed.

The only verification entry point from the old record that remains usable is `dist/semantic.min.js`. It comes from existing investigation leads and is suitable for checking whether the released output still contains rules related to the results area. Its value is in tracing back from the released behavior, not in replacing an assessment of the component's styling boundaries; seeing a block of minified rules in that file also does not directly establish that those rules are the only source or the only place to make changes.

## Status After Review

When FUI-216 was created, it stated that the output could not be reproduced reliably. A later QA review established that the behavior was reproducible, and work to address it then began. The two actions did not record the page, input, or environment conditions, so a complete set of reproduction steps cannot be reconstructed from them; however, they are enough to move this record from "retaining a hypothesis" to a decision requiring a clearly defined scope of work.

The review does not take a single reproduction with no recorded conditions to mean that all search scenarios are affected. Ordinary search results, scrollable results areas, and cases where pages add extra sizing constraints must still be assessed separately. What is addressed here is the styling behavior of the scrollable results area itself, not the automatic addition of dragging capability to every element with search in its name.

The assessment relationships used during the review are shown below. Page overrides are recorded separately only when confirmed to be independent layout exceptions; in the absence of such exceptions, first check the height and direction against the component's results-area rules.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Results area styling review" as Review
    state "Scrollable results area" as Scroll
    state "Page-local override" as Override
    state "Vertical resizing only" as Vertical
    state "Remove height cap" as Uncapped
    state "Record page rules separately" as PageRule

    [*] --> Review
    Review --> Scroll: Component results area
    Review --> Override: Confirm page exception
    Scroll --> Vertical
    Vertical --> Uncapped
    Override --> PageRule
```

The two branches in the diagram are not new implementation options. The diagram only separates boundaries already present in the initial draft: page rules may exist, but cannot replace the default assessment of the results area before they have been confirmed.

## Current Decision

Customizable Search Result Styling only applies to scrollable search results areas. The results area has no `max-height` upper limit and allows resizing only in the `vertical` direction. Fixed heights, horizontal resizing, and unconfirmed page overrides are outside the implementation scope of this decision.

Removing the height cap and limiting the resizing direction must be considered together. Keeping only the former would leave the results area uncapped without specifying what kind of size change the user can make; keeping only the latter could produce the opposite behavior, where the panel can be dragged but is still stopped by a height cap. Together they describe the usable dimensions of the results area, not the matching, sorting, or request process for search results.

This decision does not require ordinary results panels without scrolling styles to become resizable. When ordinary results need only layout styling, a drag state must not be added merely because they belong to the same search component. Nor should this decision forcibly override a page's existing explicit sizing constraints; those constraints must first be checked to determine whether they are independent layout rules of the consuming page.

The contents of the results area are not changed by this choice. Remote queries, caching, fields used for matching, and result sorting determine what is displayed, not whether the results panel can be resized vertically. Tying those settings to the sizing decision would create the false impression that changing the query method requires the panel's behavior to be decided again. The existing record establishes no such connection.

Likewise, not setting a maximum height on the results area does not mean the page as a whole is no longer subject to layout constraints. The outer container may still be affected by the page layout, overlay position, or other existing styles. This work addresses the results area's own scrolling styles; whether the outer container expands or contracts should be determined by the corresponding page's or component's own rules.

## Reasons for Rejecting Other Approaches

The approach of "first restoring a fixed height, then relaxing it when someone raises an issue with long lists" is not adopted. It defers a known sizing requirement until it becomes a later complaint; although it would make a consistent appearance easy to achieve in the short term, it cannot preserve the space that long result lists originally needed. The compatibility cost here is not an extra appearance variant, but prematurely narrowing the usable range of the results area.

The approach of "first looking for theme output, and treating the issue as nonexistent if none is found" is not adopted either. The theme may contribute to the final CSS output, but examining the theme is not a prerequisite for assessing the behavior of the results area. First check whether the results area still has a height limit and whether nonvertical resizing is allowed; only once both points conform to the decision is it worth continuing to check whether the theme output has introduced another override.

The approach of "first adding a rule to one page, then looking at other pages" is retained for exception handling rather than as the default. It is suitable for single-page layout conflicts confirmed later, but must not change the component's results-area rules without evidence of a page-specific exception. If each page adds its own override, the sizing behavior of the same search results will gradually become inconsistent.

The initial draft was too broad in treating "finding a local override" as a condition for moving the decision back to a page-level record. This is now corrected as follows: a single override can only indicate that the page may have additional rules; it cannot overturn the component-level assessment of the results area. Only when the override is confirmed to be the sole source of the original issue, and the standard scrollable results area does not exhibit the same behavior, should this record be narrowed back down to a page compatibility issue.

## Stopping Points for Follow-up Verification

For FUI-216, reproduction work has already been carried out, but no result counts, theme differences, or specific behavior after dragging were recorded. These conditions are not being filled in now. When work continues, record the search instance used, whether the results area is scrollable, and the observed states of the height and direction restrictions separately; this information is enough to determine whether the case falls within the scope of this decision.

One related question has not been split out: whether the inner area will still display as expected after its height cap is removed when a page applies sizing constraints to the outer search results container. It is not a basis for choosing a fixed height or vertical resizing, and no material identifies it as a defect. Assessment can wait until there is a specific consuming page.

DOC-26 discusses Field Error Count Limit and shares no styling decision with this record. The association is retained only to make it easier to view another API discussion from the same round of wrap-up work; neither document's conclusions should be carried over into the other.

On later review, this phrase actually conflated three things: whether the results area has a height cap, which direction the user can resize it, and whether the result content remains in the original scrolling area after the change. The first is a styling constraint, the second is the permitted interaction direction, and only the third concerns how the result content is accommodated. They cannot continue to be represented by the single phrase "the panel can be stretched."

## Trade-offs Left by the Initial Draft

Fixed height was once a candidate solution. Its advantages are that screenshots are easy to compare and it does not add a state after dragging; the problem is that it puts both long and short lists into the same box. Consistent appearance does not show that the original usable space remains, especially for a scrolling results area: an unchanged panel does not mean the user can still see or operate on more results. Therefore, fixed height is not adopted as the default treatment.

Another candidate was to attribute the issue directly to theme variables. This makes the change look small and is easy to explain as a skin difference. However, a theme can affect width, spacing, and visual hierarchy; it cannot on that basis reduce "whether resizing is allowed, which direction to resize, and whether to remove the height cap" to a theme choice. The existing material does not support this classification, so theme variables are not the anchor for this decision.

Adding an override only to a consumer page was another option. It is the most direct approach for a single page, and its impact is limited; the cost is that the same search results would have different sizing rules on different pages. The initial draft established no page exceptions, so a one-off page patch cannot be used in place of the component-level judgment. This option is reserved for pages whose layout exception can later be confirmed.

The only verification entry point from the old record that can still be used is `dist/semantic.min.js`. It comes from an existing investigation lead and is suitable for confirming whether the published output still contains rules related to the results area. Its value is in tracing backward from released behavior, not in replacing the judgment about the component's styling boundary; seeing a minified rule in that file cannot directly establish that the rule is the sole source or the only modification point.

## Status After Review

At creation, FUI-216 was recorded as meaning that the output could not be reproduced consistently. Later quality review established that the behavior was reproducible, after which it entered handling. The two actions did not preserve the page, input, or environment conditions, so a complete reproduction procedure cannot be filled in from them; however, they are sufficient to move this record from "retain the hypothesis" to a decision requiring the handling scope to be made explicit.

The review does not extrapolate one reproduction without conditions to mean that all search scenarios are affected. Ordinary search results, scrolling results areas, and cases where the page adds extra size constraints must still be assessed separately. This addresses the styling behavior of the scrolling results area itself; it does not automatically add drag capability to every element whose name contains search.

The decision relationship used during review is as follows. A page override is recorded separately only when it is confirmed to be an independent layout exception; without such an exception, first inspect the height and direction according to the component results-area rules.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Results-area style review" as Review
    state "Scrolling results area" as Scroll
    state "Page-local override" as Override
    state "Vertical adjustment only" as Vertical
    state "Remove height cap" as Uncapped
    state "Record page rule separately" as PageRule

    [*] --> Review
    Review --> Scroll: Component results area
    Review --> Override: Confirm page exception
    Scroll --> Vertical
    Vertical --> Uncapped
    Override --> PageRule
```

The two branches in the diagram are not new implementation options. They merely draw out the boundaries already present in the initial draft: page rules may exist, but they cannot replace the default results-area judgment before they are confirmed.

## Current Decision

Customizable Search Result Styling applies only to the scrolling search-results area. The results area does not impose a `max-height` limit and permits resizing only in the `vertical` direction. Fixed height, horizontal resizing, and unconfirmed page overrides are all outside the implementation scope of this decision.

Removing the height cap and limiting the resizing direction must be considered together. Retaining only the former would leave the results area uncapped without specifying which size change the user can make; retaining only the latter could produce the opposite behavior, where the panel can be dragged but is still blocked by the height cap. Together, the two describe the usable size of the results area, not the matching, sorting, or request process for search results.

This decision does not require ordinary results panels without scrolling styles to become resizable panels. When ordinary results only need layout handling, they must not gain a drag state merely because they belong to the same search component. A page that already has explicit size constraints should not be forcibly overridden by this decision; that constraint must first be confirmed as an independent consumer-side layout rule.

The result-area content itself is not changed by this choice. Remote queries, caching, matching fields, and result sorting determine what is displayed; they do not determine whether the results panel can be resized vertically. Binding these settings to the sizing decision would create the false impression that changing the query method requires deciding the panel behavior again. The existing record establishes no such association.

Likewise, not setting a maximum height on the results area does not mean that the page as a whole is no longer subject to layout constraints. The outer container may still be affected by page layout, overlay position, or other existing styles. This change addresses the scrolling style of the results area itself; whether the outer layer expands or contracts should be determined by the rules of the corresponding page or component.

## Reasons for the Paths Not Adopted

The approach of "restore a fixed height first, and open it up only after someone reports a long-list problem" is not adopted. It defers a known sizing need into a later complaint; although it can produce a consistent visual in the short term, it cannot preserve the space that a long results list originally needs. The compatibility cost here is not an additional appearance, but prematurely narrowing the usable range of the results area.

The approach of "look for the theme output first, and treat the problem as nonexistent if it cannot be found" is also not adopted. The theme side may participate in the final CSS output, but looking for the theme is not a prerequisite for determining the results-area behavior. First confirm whether the results area is still height-constrained and whether non-vertical resizing is allowed; only when both already conform to the decision is it worth continuing to check whether the theme output has introduced another override.

The approach of "add a rule to one page first, then look at the other pages" is retained for exception handling rather than as the default solution. It is suitable for a single-page layout conflict confirmed later, but it cannot change the results-area rules around the component without evidence of a page exception. If each page adds its own override, the sizing behavior of the same search results will gradually lose consistency.

The initial draft described "discovering a local override" as the condition for sending the decision back to the page record; this wording was too broad. The correction is: a single override can only show that the page may have an additional rule; it cannot overturn the component-level results-area judgment. Only when it is confirmed that the override is the sole source of the original issue, and that the standard scrolling results area does not exhibit the same behavior, should this record be narrowed back to a page-compatibility issue.

## Stop Point for Follow-up Verification

FUI-216 already includes reproduction actions, but it does not record the result count, theme differences, or the specific behavior after dragging. These conditions are not to be filled in now. When proceeding, record the search instance used, whether the results area has scrolling, and the states observed separately for the height constraint and the direction constraint; this information is sufficient to determine whether it is covered by this decision.

One adjacent issue has not been split off: when a page sets a size constraint on the outer layer of the search results, whether removing the height cap from the inner layer still displays as expected. It is not a basis for choosing fixed height or vertical resizing, and no material identifies it as a defect. Assess it once a specific consumer page appears.

DOC-26 discusses Field Error Count Limit, and it shares no styling decision with this record. The association is retained only to make it easier to view another interface discussion closed out in the same round; the conclusions of the two materials should not be carried into each other.

## 2.9 Closeout Ruling (2026-09-26, currently authoritative)

The resizable styling is limited to search components that have all four classes—ui, search, scrolling, and resizable; their direct child .results must remain scrollable, with resize: vertical and max-height: none. Ordinary scrolling (without resizable, including category variants) must retain its original responsive height cap and must not be resizable; resizable without scrolling, ordinary search, and unrelated .results must not gain this capability. Class order and additional category markers do not matter; mobile, tablet, and desktop widths all follow this scope.

# Field Error Count Limit Proposal

In 2.9 Cumulative Behavior Closeout, there isn't yet a separate policy for handling the number of field errors. The aim here isn't to switch to a different set of validation rules, but to see whether the form can still keep users focused on what matters when there are many errors.

Three options to start with:

1. Limit only the number of errors shown in the error summary area; fields themselves retain their existing error information.
2. Truncate field errors as they are collected, so downstream rendering only sees the truncated set.
3. Set no cap on the number of errors; only adjust the error summary's readability.

Option 1 looks like the smallest change, but we need to confirm that hidden errors won't lead callers to think the fields have passed validation. Option 2 turns a presentation problem into a data problem; it shouldn't be the first choice unless the existing form error collection is already consumed only once. Option 3 doesn't require a new boundary, but it doesn't address long error lists crowding out the form.

The tentative preference is to start with a small-scale trial of option 1: the cap applies only to the summary display, with no changes to individual field messages or validation results. The criteria for dropping this approach are also defined up front: if the same set of field errors produces different form validity results before and after applying the cap, or if callers can no longer access the original field errors, stop pursuing this approach.

No numeric cap has been decided yet. We first need to check whether errors are counted per field or per server-side error; the two methods yield different counts when one field has multiple errors.
